items.title: HECM endorsements rebound in October but stay near decade low
items.description: The federally insured reverse mortgage market posted a rebound in October, but activity remained at historically low levels compared to the past decade, according to data compiled by Reverse Market Insight (RMI) and published Friday by HECMWorld.com. Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) endorsements rose to 1,995 in October, an 11% increase from September and the highest level in three months, the data shows. But even with the gain, this was the lowest figure for the month of October in at least 10 years. Year to date, endorsements are about 3.19% below last year’s level — but comparisons are complicated by the federal government shutdown in October 2025, which disrupted activity and reporting. Finance of America Reverse (FOA) remained the top HECM lender in October with 460 endorsements, followed by Longbridge Financial with 362 and Mutual of Omaha Mortgage with 332. Goodlife Home Loans posted 110 endorsements and Fairway Home Mortgage recorded 67. Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha switched positions from September, and Goodlife jumped three spots by originating 62 more HECMs compared to the prior month. The top three lenders accounted for about 63% of all HECM endorsements in October, underscoring how concentrated the reverse mortgage business has become. The number of active lenders with more than one HECM endorsement improved, rising to 75 in October from 63 in September. From January through October, FOA widened its lead with 4,398 endorsements. Mutual of Omaha ranked second with 4,041, followed by Longbridge at 3,513, Goodlife at 916 and South River Mortgage at 692. HMBS issuance While endorsements increased, securitization volume moved in the opposite direction. HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities (HMBS) issuance in October was down 16% from September. New View Advisors , citing its analysis of data from Ginnie Mae and private sources, reported that October HMBS issuance totaled $419 million, a decline of $27 million from September. There were 61 pools issued in October, nine fewer than in September. FOA led all issuers in October with $180 million in HMBS issuance, up from $175 million in September. Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha saw month-over-month declines, issuing $116 million and $76 million, respectively. First-participation pool production dropped to $238 million in October, down $28 million from September and $97 million from October 2025. New View said issuers “continue to struggle with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%.” From January to October, FOA was the top first-participation HMBS issuer with $1.01 billion of issuance, according to New View. Longbridge followed at $863 million and Mutual of Omaha at $593 million. In October, the 61 HMBS pools consisted of 14 first-participation pools and 47 tail pools. New View also highlighted the ongoing use of very small pools as 18 of the October pools had an aggregate size below $1 million, totaling $10.8 million of unpaid principal balance that might not otherwise have been issued. items.title: Century Communities names Jim Francescon as president
items.description: Century Communities Inc. (NYSE: CCS) announced on Monday that Jim Francescon has been promoted to president, effective Jan. 1, 2027, as part of the company’s long-term succession planning process. The company, ranked 13th by sales volume in the HousingWire Homebuilder Rankings , said Dale Francescon will continue to serve as executive chairman. Rob Francescon, who currently serves as chief executive officer and president, will remain CEO. As president, Jim Francescon will oversee Century Communities’ homebuilding operations, land and related corporate functions and will help drive the company’s strategy and growth, according to the announcement. “Today’s announcement reflects the implementation of a succession plan that our Board, Rob, and I have been planning and executing over the past two years,” Dale Francescon, executive chairman of Century Communities, said in a statement. “We have been very thoughtful in how we have approached succession, with the goal of best positioning Century for long-term alignment with shareholders, success and growth.” “Jim has played an integral role in shaping our strategic direction and our growth into one of the largest homebuilders in the country, including leading our recent acquisitions that have deepened our footprint and strengthened our platform,” Rob Francescon, CEO of Century Communities, said. “I look forward to continuing to work closely with Jim and our entire executive team as we position Century for continued success.” Jim Francescon said he is “honored to take on this role and grateful to our Board, Dale and Rob for their confidence.” “We have built a strong operating platform and a talented team, and I am excited about the opportunities ahead as we continue to grow and deliver on our promise of A Home for Every Dream®,” he said. Francescon joined Century Communities in 2019 and most recently served as executive vice president, corporate operations, overseeing much of the company’s corporate operations, including homebuilding, land, strategy, business development, and mergers and acquisitions. In that role, he led the company’s acquisition strategy, including recent acquisitions of HistoryMaker Homes , Anglia Homes and Landmark Homes of Tennessee , which expanded Century’s presence in Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Nashville, respectively. Before serving as executive vice president, Francescon was president of Century Living, the company’s multifamily platform, and earlier served as corporate vice president. Prior to joining Century, he worked in private equity at GoldPoint Partners, a subsidiary of New York Life Investments, and in investment banking at J.P. Morgan Securities LLC. He holds a Bachelor of Science in business administration with a concentration in finance and real estate and a Master of Science in finance from the University of Denver. Francescon also serves as a trustee of the University of Denver, Children’s Hospital Colorado Foundation and ACE Scholarships Colorado. Related More: Homebuilders

items.description: Title waivers going national soon Pulte says; UWM, Rate already in By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published November 09, 2026, 4:16 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Processing Content Forward Look: Prepare for updates on the program's expansion in early December. Expert Quote: "As policymakers continue addressing the nation's housing affordability challenges, consumer protection must remain part of the conversation," — Chris Morton, ALTA CEO Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. The expansion of government-sponsored enterprise Fannie Mae's title waiver pilot is on track to make more progress next month, according to Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte. "We are actively working, per the President's executive order , to expand the title insurance pilot program across the United States," FHFA Director Bill Pulte said in a social media post on X late Friday. "We will be publishing updates in early December." That means that the current pilot — which is currently limited to certain loans, regions and lenders like UWM and Rate — will be made broadly available despite some wariness from Congress and the title industry. The executive order also calls for it to be made a permanent program. If this happens, certain refinances deemed to have low title risk won't need title insurance or attorney opinion letters with the aim of reducing borrowers' closing costs, according to Fannie's description of the pilot. One potential hurdle to or restriction on this may come from a bipartisan group within Congress. A pair of legislators, both of which have been re-elected, proposed strict guardrails on the program beyond its current limited availability. The American Land Title Association on Monday urged members of Congress to review lien-related risks as they engage in lawmaking with the midterms behind them. "As policymakers continue addressing the nation's housing affordability challenges, consumer protection must remain part of the conversation," ALTA CEO Chris Morton said in a press statement commenting on Congress's post-midterm agenda. Lawmakers have proposed legislation to this end in the past. Title waivers' history in Congress and at the FHFA Rep. Andrew Gabarino, R-N.Y., and Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas, introduced a bill in 2025 that would require all enterprise mortgages to have state-regulated insurance covering title risk or meet a minimal capital requirement for an additional 1% of the unpaid principal balance The bill has gotten some broader support within Congress but not enough to move forward, and it's unclear whether Democrats' increased influence next year would change that. The title waiver push originated during the Biden administration and Pulte's predecessor, former FHFA Director Sandra Thompson, faced some opposition by a bipartisan group of legislators then , too, but more regarding the notification process around the pilot. Thompson responded by setting up pilot transparency pages at the enterprises. Fannie's currently lists the title pilot as the only ongoing one with authorization through November of next year. Fannie's current pilot transparency page indicates that it gets updated twice a year, with new projects launched in between reporting periods added within 30 days of launch. The current one indicates the title waiver pilot is authorized through November of next year. Mortgage lenders should keep a close eye on current GSE rules as policy evolves and weigh potential efficiencies from waivers, which can save up to $2,000 per loan, against potential title-fraud risk , which is rate on insured loans and has an $207,000 average cost. "Affordability and consumer protection should go hand in hand, and the title industry looks forward to working with elected officials across the country to advance commonsense solutions that lower costs while preserving the safeguards," Morton said Lenders that have reported piloting title waivers have included United Wholesale Mortgage and Rate. items.title: Joanna Gaines Says an ‘Upset’ Buyer Lost Interest in Magnolia’s $7 Million Mansion Renovation Because She Preferred the ‘Before’ Photos
items.description: Joanna Gaines has had a successful career, thanks to her signature design aesthetic, but a recent real estate snafu served as a brutal reminder that not everyone has the same taste. During an appearance on Kylie Kelce ’s podcast , “Not Gonna Lie,” the “Fixer Upper” star revealed that her most involved renovation yet lost a buyer who much preferred the “before” photos. Joanna and her husband, Chip Gaines , recently tackled the transformation of a 15,000-square-foot mansion in their hometown of Waco, TX . The process was documented in the upcoming Magnolia Network show “ Fixer Upper: Chip Bought a Mansion ,” and it appears the project was quite the struggle. While the Gaineses are a solid team, Chip actually purchased the sprawling estate without Joanna, a decision she called a “bold move.” Although the mom of five vouched the property would “never be a fixer,” she changed her mind after the property lingered on the market without much interest for more than three years. The 1990s-built palace is in an incredible location, set on a 5.7-acre lot boasting striking views of Lake Waco. But the outdated ‘90s interiors needed a serious face-lift, and when Chip and Joanna set out to work their magic on the abode, they realized it needed more work than they had anticipated. Loading... Joanna Gaines appeared on a recent episode of Kylie Kelce's podcast, "Not Gonna Lie," and shared a surprising story about her latest show. YouTube/Not Gonna Lie with Kylie Kelce Loading... The upcoming series "Fixer Upper: Chip Bought a Mansion" follows the couple as they transform a huge mansion. Magnolia Network Loading... Chip purchased the home three years ago without Joanna, and now that they've renovated it, they're trying to find a buyer. Magnolia Network The process was grueling, but to add insult to injury, an interaction with an interested buyer made it seem like it was all for nothing. “If you look online, the pictures you see is of the ‘before,’” Joanna said. The listing , held by Amanda Nesbitt of Magnolia Realty , keeps the “after” images a secret to avoid spoiling the show. In a twist of fate, the prospective buyer had fallen in love with the outdated photos in the listing and was disappointed to learn that Chip and Joanna had stripped the home of its former McMansion glory. Joanna recalled that on “the day of the reveal,” the real estate agents called to let the Gaineses know that a “qualified buyer” had “fallen in love” with the estate and wanted to put an offer in. The HGTV personality offered to give the buyer a walk through the home to chat about the changes they had made, only to realize that the renovation was a deal breaker. “She said, ‘Well, what did they do?’ She was like, ‘I liked the pictures that I saw,’” Joanna said. Loading... On the day of the reveal, a potential buyer who loved the before photos (listed here) was "upset" to see the Gaineses had changed the home. Realtor.com Loading... The 15,000-square-foot abode has an interior that would be outdated to some, but the prospective buyer preferred it. Realtor.com Loading... The listing photos show only the "before" version of the home to avoid spoiling the show, so Joanna offered to personally walk the buyer through the property. Realtor.com Loading... She wasn't interested and refused to even come to a viewing, noting that she had preferred the original look. Realtor.com Loading... The series premieres on Dec. 27, giving fans a chance to see what Chip and Joanna have decided to do with the home. Realtor.com Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to retain the buyer, who decided not to come for the viewing at all. “The lady was so upset,” Joanna recalled. “She was like, ‘I don’t understand why she removed all the red and gold.’” “It’s like, Chip was right,” she continued. “He could have sold this thing as is. We didn’t have to touch it. I’m like, ‘This is a joke.' I finally did it. I revealed it, and now we have a buyer and she’s upset that I fixed it up.” The six-bedroom, 11-bathroom mansion is still on the market, asking $7.39 million. Although the new furnishings are still under wraps, viewers can get a look when the series premieres on Dec. 27 on Magnolia Network and HGTV. The missed opportunity wasn’t the only revelation Joanna shared on the podcast episode. She also divulged that lately, she and Chip have been discussing expanding the family. “When I had Crew at 40, I said, ‘Chip, I want him to have more siblings,’” she said. “I really thought I’d have nine children. I’m that lady. Look at my hair. Don’t I look like a lady that would have nine kids? And he was not open to it. Guess who’s open to it now? At 48?” Joanna went on to share that her husband is “telling everyone” that she’s pregnant, even though she is not. From their adult children to a crowd of 2,000 people at a recent speaking engagement, Chip has continued to share the false news in an attempt to “speak it out into the universe.” “So that whole audience thinks I’m pregnant. I don’t know what’s happening, but I’m not,” she confirmed. Get real estate news in your inbox Sign up now Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. items.title: 3 multifamily groundbreakings you may have missed
items.description: 3 multifamily groundbreakings you may have missed Construction has started on apartment projects in California, Texas and Pennsylvania. Published Nov. 9, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Lincoln Property Co. and McCourt Partners broke ground Nov. 5 on ElevenOneEleven in Culver City, Calif. Courtesy of Lincoln Property Co. and McCourt Partners Several multifamily projects broke ground around the country in the first week of November. Lincoln Property Co. and McCourt Partners started a development called ElevenOneEleven in Culver City, California, one of the strongest rental markets in Southern California, according to Stephen Lindgren, senior vice president and Los Angeles market leader at Lincoln. Like much of the SoCal region, Culver City needs more housing, but “as with any new housing development of this scale, the entitlement process and rising construction costs can present challenges,” Lindgren said in emailed comments. However, “Culver City leaders have recognized the need to create a supportive environment for new residential development,” Lindgren said. “That partnership has been instrumental in advancing ElevenOneEleven.” Here is more detail about the ElevenOneEleven project and two other newly launched developments in Texas and Pennsylvania. ElevenOneEleven in Culver City, California On Thursday, Lincoln and McCourt Partners started construction on a six-story, mixed-use development in the Los Angeles area close to major employers and “convenient access to the best West LA lifestyle amenities,” according to a press release shared with Multifamily Dive. The project price tag is $200 million , the Los Angeles Times reported. The development will bring 344 apartments, including 52 affordable units. In addition, it will include 2,000 square feet of retail and 17,520 square feet of publicly accessible outdoor space. Amenities will include a resident club with a sports simulator and gaming lounge; a private courtyard with a pool, grills and a movie screening area; a fitness center with a sauna; a coworking space; and an outdoor lounge, per the release. One of the project's most compelling aspects is the opportunity to make a meaningful impact on a long underutilized site, according to McCourt Partners President Jordan Lang. “We're excited to introduce significant new housing inventory in an established market at a time when opportunities to develop at this scale are limited,” Lang said in emailed comments. “We've approached the project with the understanding that successful development should extend beyond the building, creating spaces and amenities that enhance and activate the surrounding neighborhood.” KFA Architects designed the project, Kimley-Horn is the civil engineer and Allen Matkins represented the project on land use matters, according to the release. Work is expected to wrap up in the fourth quarter of 2028. Twenty-Twelve in Philadelphia Optional Caption Retrieved from JKRP Architects on November 09, 2026 The Philadelphia Housing Authority, Alterra Property Group and RHEAL Capital Management broke ground Friday on a $62.5 million , 14-story mixed-income community with 121 apartments and 2,000 square feet of ground-floor commercial space, according to a press release. Alterra will build and manage the development under a 99-year ground lease structure on behalf of PHA, the owner. The project transforms the former site of PHA’s administrative headquarters and marks the agency’s first residential property in Philadelphia’s Center City district, per the release. Sixty percent of the homes will be reserved for families earning up to 80% of the Area Median Income, while the remaining 40% will rent at market rate. “Admittedly, the road to get here faced its share of hurdles, nearly two decades of vision, redesigns, and navigating federal approvals,” PHA President and CEO Kelvin Jeremiah said in the release. “This landmark development reflects our commitment to ensuring that affordable, high-quality housing is available in every part of the city.” Twenty-Twelve’s downtown location will offer residents easy access to jobs, transit and schools, per the release. The building is equipped with a rooftop terrace, a fitness center and technology-enabled meeting rooms on each floor. The project is slated for completion by Q4 2028. Mid-rise apartments in Dallas Optional Caption Courtesy of Trademark Property Co. and Morgan Group Co-general partners Trademark Property Co. and Morgan Group started construction Wednesday on a 362-unit, class A multifamily project in Dallas’ Oak Lawn neighborhood that will occupy an entire 3-acre city block, according to a press release. Morgan is also the project’s developer, general contractor and property manager. “Getting this development to this point took many years of hard work, collaboration and persistence, and we are thrilled to reach this milestone,” Chad Colley, multifamily and mixed-use partner at Trademark Property, said in the release. The podium-style community will consist of three-, five- and seven-story building components with studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom floor plans. The residences will have premium finishes, in-unit washers and dryers and walk-in closets. Some will offer dens, balconies or large private patios, and certain ground-level homes will have private yards. Amenities will include a rooftop pool and outdoor spa; a fitness center with a private studio, sauna and cold plunge; a pocket park and courtyards; a clubroom and coffee bar; coworking areas; a golf simulator and virtual gaming area; a dog park and dog wash; EV charging stations; cold storage for food deliveries; a package room with return-valet service; and indoor bike storage. GFF is the project architect, SJL Design Group is the interior designer and LandDesign is the landscape architect. items.title: NAR sees pent-up demand waiting on lower mortgage rates, better sentiment
items.description: The U.S. housing market is building “significant” pent-up demand that could be released if mortgage rates ease, inventory improves and consumer confidence rebounds, National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) chief economist Lawrence Yun told attendees Friday at NAR’s NXT in New Orleans. Yun contrasted today’s sales environmen t with the year 2000, noting that the U.S. population has grown from 281 million to 350 million and payroll jobs from 132 million to 159 million over that period. Housing wealth has ballooned from $7 trillion to $35 trillion, yet existing-home sales are tracking near 4 million this year , well below the 5.2 million homes sold in 2000, he said, citing NAR data. “Affordability is tough, but people’s incomes are rising, and if somehow mortgage rates go down, think about the potential housing demand that could be released to the marketplace,” Yun said. On the supply side, Yun said inventory has risen as sales have slowed. Months’ supply is now at its highest level since 2015, and the median home took 33 days to go from listing to contract in September, according to NAR. “Homes are staying on the market a little longer than before,” Yun said. “With longer days on market, you have to be realistic to the market condition. Otherwise, buyers will reject the homes on the market.” Yun pointed to consumer psychology as a key missing ingredient. Consumer sentiment has fallen to roughly half its 2000 level and is now worse than during the Great Recession, even as the labor market has added jobs. “If we can boost confidence levels, maybe that can also change the dynamics,” Yun said. First-time buyers remain near historic lows Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research, presented findings from the trade group’s newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers . First-time buyers made up 22% of all buyers, near the series low, and the median age of first-time buyers held at a record-high 40. Those numbers underscore how younger households are delaying homeownership, even as they form households and enter peak earning years. For lenders and real estate brokerages, that means fewer entry-level transactions and more emphasis on move-up or equity-rich buyers. “ First-time home buyers are struggling,” Lautz said. “They’re not struggling just with housing affordability. They're also struggling with rent. They’re struggling with student loan debt, and a rising issue for first-time home buyers is childcare costs.” Lautz noted that sellers reported staying in their homes for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest tenure on record for the survey. “The golden handcuffs of low interest rate mortgages is true. People are holding on to those properties for longer periods of time,” she said. “It’s why we need to build more housing inventory—especially affordable housing inventory—for the potential first-time home buyers who are out there.” Agent usage hits record highs Despite technology and direct-to-consumer platforms, use of licensed professionals in transactions remained strong, according to NAR’s survey. A reported 90% of buyers purchased through an agent, the highest share in four decades, and a record 92% of sellers used an agent. “Sellers want agents to price that home competitively, find that qualified buyer, help with marketing, and make sure they get to the closing table in a time frame that they need to do so,” Lautz said. Why this matters for housing professionals For real estate agents and brokers, NAR’s data point to a market where transaction volume is constrained more by affordability, rates and sentiment than by underlying demand. A larger population, more jobs and higher housing wealth suggest that activity could accelerate quickly if mortgage rates retreat and confidence improves. For lenders, a 22% first-time buyer share and a median first-time buyer age of 40 highlight both near-term headwinds and an eventual backlog of delayed demand. Households that are renting longer and juggling student debt and childcare may respond strongly to any easing in rates, pricing or down payment constraints. For builders and developers, Lautz’s comments reinforce the policy and business case for adding affordable inventory . With existing owners locked in by sub-4% mortgages and staying put for a median 12 years, new construction remains one of the few levers to ease the entry-level shortage. Yun’s and Lautz’s remarks come as the industry also adjusts to p ost-settlement commission rule changes and elevated borrowing costs , making accurate pricing, counseling on affordability and clear communication with consumers more central to winning business in 2027 and beyond. items.title: What NAR's new MLS policy options mean for data feeds and licensing
items.description: The National Association of Realtors (NAR) has approved four multiple listing service (MLS) policy recommendations that increase MLSs’ options to claim copyright in listing content, expand local flexibility on data feeds, clarify permissible uses of MLS data and update qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee. The recommendations from NAR’s Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee were considered and adopted at NAR NXT 2026 conference on Sunday and are tied to the trade group’s 2026-2028 strategic plan to modernize MLS policies, the association said in an announcement Sunday. New optional copyright policy for MLS data The most consequential change for brokers and MLS operators is a revision to MLS Policy Statement 7.85 and the creation of a new optional policy on copyright protection of MLS data. Under the revised policy, MLSs may, at their discretion, require up to a 50% copyright interest in certain listing content to strengthen copyright enforcement, subject to quarterly copyright registration requirements. MLSs must give participants the right to opt out of assigning a copyright interest to the MLS, and brokers retain the right to independently use and license their own listing content. Copyright ownership and enforcement have become more important as listing photos and data are syndicated across portals, IDX sites and marketing platforms, and as MLSs face more frequent questions and disputes about unauthorized scraping and reuse of listing content. Greater local flexibility on data feeds NAR also adopted an optional MLS policy on MLS data feed services. The policy allows MLSs to establish local eligibility and licensing requirements for data feeds, as long as those rules are reasonable, objective and applied equally to all participants. Even with new local rules, participants must retain access to MLS listing information and data feeds for their own listings. For brokers and vendors, this could affect how quickly and under what conditions they can obtain broader data feeds for tools such as brokerage websites, back-office systems and analytics products, depending on how individual MLSs choose to implement the optional policy. Clarification on permitted MLS data uses A new MLS policy statement reinforces that the use of MLS data must comply with applicable MLS participation or data licensing agreements and must be connected to real estate brokerage services, the preparation of appraisals or other valuations of real property. NAR said this is intended to address concerns around unauthorized use of MLS content, including use cases that are not connected to providing brokerage or valuation services. For MLSs, this language provides additional backing for enforcement actions against parties that use listing data for unrelated commercial purposes. For brokers and appraisers, it underscores the need to align technology partnerships and data workflows with the scope of their MLS agreements. Updated qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee NAR also updated the qualification criteria for service on its MLS Committee. The changes are meant to better reflect today’s MLS environment and ensure the committee includes members with relevant industry expertise and perspectives. While specific qualification details were not outlined in the announcement, changes to committee composition can influence how future policy recommendations are shaped and how regional and business-model interests are represented at the national level. “These updates reflect our commitment to ensuring MLS policies remain relevant, effective, and responsive to the needs of today’s real estate industry,” Nykia Wright, the CEO of NAR and a 2026 HousingWire Woman of Influence and Vanguard award winner, said in the announcement. “In line with our 2026–2028 Strategic Plan and significant member feedback, we will continue working collaboratively with MLSs, brokers, members, and other industry partners to support a clear understanding and implementation of these changes.” Next steps for MLSs and brokers Because several of the policies are optional , local MLSs will have to decide whether and how to adopt them. MLS executives and boards will likely review their copyright strategies, data feed agreements and committee engagement structures in light of the new framework. Brokers, teams and technology vendors should review their MLS participation and data licensing agreements to understand how any local policy changes could affect website data feeds, marketing uses of listing content and third-party integrations. items.title: 'Certainty Will Be The Buzzword': Stability, Not Sea Change, For CRE Post-Midterm
items.description: The implications of an overwhelming Democratic midterm victory reverberated through markets in the second half of last week, reflecting skittishness among investors and business leaders over fears about the impact on the largest driver of today's economy: data center growth. Despite these initial shocks, there is a quiet expectation that a Democratic Congress will help bring calm to a period of significant economic volatility stemming in part from the unpredictable policymaking that has emerged during President Donald Trump 's second term. “Maybe ‘uncertainty’ was the buzzword of the last year, and hopefully ‘certainty’ will be the buzzword going forward,” said Jeff DeBoer , CEO of the Washington, D.C.-based trade group The Real Estate Roundtable . “We're much more certain that we're not going to wake up every day and have another wild fluctuation in some sort of policy.” Unsplash/Sebastian Schuster That semblance of certainty won't be a panacea, however. Major relief from the ubiquitous issues for commercial real estate today, including higher costs, low labor availability and expensive debt, is unlikely to come from the new Congress because those issues are closely tied to Trump's executive actions and powers. But housing affordability, the economy more generally and data centers were on the ballot in races around the country, where the results have set the stage for a string of policy debates that will hit landlords and investors. “If you look back in history, there are a number of examples where a great amount of very positive legislation has been done when there's divided government,” DeBoer said. “I'm not one who says, ‘Put your feet up, nothing's going to happen, we're in for gridlock.’ I think there's going to be some significant legislation.” Stock traders initially reacted positively to the midterm results, with all three major indexes climbing, but the mood changed Thursday. A massive sell-off focused on tech stocks but spread marketwide sucked $2.5T in market value out of the Nasdaq and pushed the index into correction territory. By Friday, the dust had settled and markets opened by gaining back some of Thursday’s losses. Investors are trying to reprice their bets on the pace of the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out as they weigh the prospect of a Congress that is more skeptical of the major tech firms’ plans and a wave of local fervor against data centers that drove voters to the polls. AI and data centers emerged as a key political flashpoint, with more than half of respondents telling an NBC exit poll that it was a crucial or major factor in their decision to vote in the midterms. Across statewide races and referendums, voters roundly supported measures putting limits on data center development in more than 40 local ballot measures . “This election, whether federally or on the local level, was influenced by data centers,” said Commercial Real Estate Development Association CEO Marc Selvitelli. “This was the rare bipartisan issue that was out there right now.” The economy emerged as the top issue for voters headed into the election after the U.S. war with Iran drove up energy costs and added to already elevated inflation. The president’s tariffs are also contributing to the rising costs, but the Democratic sweep in Congress still has limited reach into trade policy that’s coming directly from the White House. "The swing in Congress, the results of the election, are very unlikely to have a significant impact on the president's trade agenda and the tariffs that are in place," Blake Harden, managing director for trade policy at ​ Ernst & Young 's Washington Council office, told Reuters . "This is because there is so much trade authority within the executive branch that's been delegated by Congress." Unsplash/Jesse Paul Democrats have floated the idea of changing the tariff laws the president is relying on to impose his protectionist trade regime, but the party would need to win over some Republicans because it remains short of a veto-proof majority. They’re also working on a plan to roll back Trump’s tariffs directed at Canada, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday. “The midterm election results are unlikely to materially influence commercial real estate performance,” Cushman & Wakefield analysts wrote in a postelection report . A divided government adds some degree of fiscal policy stability that “should be calming for markets,” although the U.S. war in Iran and the downstream impacts on prices and inflation remain the greatest “swing factor for inflation and rates,” they wrote. The election was at least in part a referendum on the war in Iran, according to Hans Nordby , executive managing director of research and investment analytics at Transwestern . “And it was a ‘no’ vote,” Nordby wrote in an email to Bisnow on Friday. “The new Congress could defund the war or otherwise force a withdrawal. If that were to happen, it would seem likely that oil prices could retreat to prewar levels, which would put downward pressure on inflation.” The war and its economic fallout, particularly on the price of oil, has been a thorn in CRE's side since it broke out in February. The rising cost of oil has contributed to overall inflation remaining elevated, which in turn has kept borrowing rates higher. Yields for 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds , a key benchmark rate for all sorts of debt costs, notched lower following the midterms after climbing above 5% in October before retreating, shedding 6 basis points Wednesday and continuing to trade below 4.9% through Friday. The shift in Congress likely sets the stage for bitter political fights between Trump and Democrats, some of whom have pledged to launch investigations into the White House. items.title: Can the new Congress help lower mortgage rates?
items.description: After the Democrats' historic midterm win , the question now is: can the new Congress help get mortgage rates lower? Obviously, the Iran conflict and trade war have taken their toll on President Trump's approval ratings, but can Congress — both Democrats and Republicans — now work together on getting something done that the President will not veto? Let's look at the economic factors influencing rates in this environment, what Congress can do about each, and how the Fed might consider these as they set monetary policy. 1. Oil and diesel prices When WTI oil was at $112 on April 7 this year, the 10-year yield was at 4.31% — but back then the Fed was still talking about cutting rates two to three times. A lot has changed since then. The Federal Reserve has made the Iran conflict a big talking point, so some type of resolution to this conflict could impact rates. Obviously, the conflict has hurt President Trump and the Republicans; it’s very unpopular, especially with farmers and truckers who have to deal with high diesel prices. Trump himself acknowledged the war played a major part in the midterm results. Congress made some attempts to try to end this conflict in the past, but may have renewed incentives now to find a solution. We shall see what comes next, as President Trump has said he could make a deal after the midterms. 2. The AI boom Now, the AI boom is a little bit more complicated because there are a lot of projects still in the pipeline that can’t be shut down by the Democrats right now, but future projects could definitely be affected. And with some type of regulation and moratorium, some of the growth prospects might be slowed down. This is a critical factor because the Federal Reserve has really made the AI boom and inflation a hot topic. It’s part of the reason why, when you see AI softness — whether it’s the credit markets or their stock prices getting hit — bond traders tend to want to buy bonds, not sell them, in that environment. For now, the Fed needs to see a material slowdown to lose its hawkish stance on AI, but it would be another positive for rates. On another note, the labor productivity data was awesome today. This data really affects how the Fed sees AI and will be the best news for mortgage rates if this trend continues. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh himself has made a dovish case around AI as long as it creates more productivity and lowers labor unit costs. Here is the chart of the 10-year yield for the last six months as of this second, the 10-year yield is down once again to 4.83% as AI stocks are selling off. 3. Trade war 2.0 This will be very interesting because I am sure President Trump will try every legal angle to continue his tariff policy — he still wants to have tariffs because it’s his favorite tool to cut deals. However, what the midterms have done is limit the power he can have to escalate the trade war into something worse. That can be a very big positive: we might have seen the high of the 10-year yield at 5.35% if the trade war doesn’t get worse amid the conflict with Iran. For now, we need to wait and see how much farther the President wants to push the trade war. He might just cut a deal with Canada, leave other countries alone and just focus on China — which would be a positive for rates. 4. Jobs Usually, in an economic cycle, when manufacturing jobs and construction jobs are being lost, it’s not a good sign for the labor market: we saw that in 2025. But the labor market has improved this year and that has kept the Fed's focus fully on inflation. One thing to think about going forward is that, if we do have some data center moratoriums and rates stay elevated, construction labor might get hit a little bit harder than before the midterms. If the unemployment rate rises as growth slows down, that will be a positive for mortgage rates. Conclusion For rates to really make a meaningful move lower and stick, three of the four things above need to get better. You need to get oil prices trading between $67 and $82. You need to get diesel prices down so the Fed won’t talk about energy prices being passed onto the consumer. You've got to de-escalate the trade war 2.0 and get some deals in and not make it inflationary. The AI moratorium and regulations will be a welcome signal to the Federal Reserve; whether that impacts the construction data enough to matter to them is still an open question, but the three things above need to occur to have rates go under 7% and stay there. items.title: RealPRO Select helps lift Realtor.com revenue
items.description: Move , the parent company of Realtor.com , said the momentum generated by RealPRO Select in fiscal year 2026 has carried over into the first quarter of fiscal year 2027. During the first quarter of FY 2027, Realtor.com recorded $160 million in revenue, up 5% year over year, marking the segment’s eighth consecutive quarter of growth. These financial results were highlighted during News Corp ’s fiscal year 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call on Wednesday evening. “In a housing market constrained by 7%-plus mortgage rates , Damian [Eales] and the team have exhibited exceptional discipline in their operational focus and AI integration, and that approach has converted revenue growth into meaningful bottom-line expansion,” Robert Thomson, the CEO of News Corp, said during the earnings call. RealPRO Select grows News Corp executives attributed Realtor.com ’s strong revenue performance to the growth of RealPRO Select. The company said it is focused on enhancing the platform with stronger lead generation, branding, productivity tools and training capabilities. Realtor.com also focused on the expansion of RealAssist AI during Q1, including the launch of a pilot of RealAssist in Rich Communication Services (RCS), integrated directly into Google search and available on iOS and Android. “The pilot is already attracting new users, driving strong engagement, and helping us capture pre-search intent earlier in the buyer journey before consumers ever enter a browser,” Damian Eales, the CEO of Move, wrote in a blog post about the company's quarterly performance. In addition, Realtor.com also launched RealAssist AI for Realtor.com+, which Eales said helps agents onboard their clients faster, build more tailored searches, summarize client activity and draft follow-ups in their own voice. “The platform is already supporting thousands of successful agent-client connections, and early feedback on these AI tools has been very positive,” Eales wrote. Other highlights Eales also highlighted the relaunch of the My Home dashboard, which now includes a collaboration with Opendoor . Eales said this is encouraging sellers to engage a listing agent much earlier in their journey. In addition, News Corp also noted that Comscore data shows 4.9 visits per unique user to Realtor.com, up 8% annually, and an average of 263 million monthly visits in the quarter, which the company said represents a “substantial” lead over Redfin and Homes.com . Despite these strong numbers, Realtor.com noted that lead volume was down 11%, which the portal attributed to broader market conditions and its repositioning of customer acquisitions to higher-quality and higher-value leads. “Despite a constrained housing market , Realtor.com’s strategy is delivering positive results, and we’re well positioned to grow as conditions improve,” Eales wrote. “Our focus remains on investing in our audience and AI tools that enhance a consumer’s experience and augment the role of the professional agent.” Overall, News Corp’s digital real estate services segment generated $529 million in revenue, up 10% from a year prior. The company as a whole generated $2.28 billion in revenue, a 6% annual increase, and net income of $215 million, up 43% compared to a year prior. Related More: Earnings News Corp. Realtor.com

items.title: American Housing Corp names leadership for new Austin division
items.description: The American Housing Corporation launched an Austin homebuilding division and named three industry veterans to lead the new operation as it ramps up an infill-focused, prefabricated rowhome platform, the company announced this week. Austin is the launch market for the company’s infill homebuilding strategy, which centers on designing, manufacturing and constructing urban rowhomes. The move comes as builders look for ways to add “missing middle” housing in supply-constrained, high-cost markets without relying solely on traditional greenfield development. Parker Scott, a former division president at LGI Homes , was appointed general manager, Daniel Green will serve as director of construction operations and Luke Allen will serve as director of land. Scott brings more than 20 years of homebuilding sales and operational experience to the role. Green joins from senior construction positions at Homebound , ATCO Structures and Perry Homes , where he focused on building operations and execution systems. Allen, who previously held land roles at Lennar and Ashton Woods , will oversee land acquisition, underwriting and pipeline development for the Austin market. In October 2026, American Housing Corp completed its “Demo 2” prototype using a componentized, prefabricated building system. The company is building a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing plant in Southeast Austin designed to produce up to 1,200 homes annually, according to the announcement. The factory-scale approach is intended to standardize production, shorten build times and provide more cost certainty, which could appeal to capital providers and municipalities looking for scalable infill housing solutions. For real estate investors and lenders, the combination of an infill land strategy with a controlled-offsite construction environment could change underwriting assumptions around cycle times and construction risk. Alongside the Austin division launch, the company restructured its real estate operations and parted ways with co-founder Bobby Fijan. The firm credited Fijan with helping establish its early real estate footprint and championing urban, family-sized housing. Related More: homebuilder Texas

items.title: Bobby Flay and Brooke Williamson Reveal What It’s Like To Have 2 Celebrity Chefs in a Home Kitchen—and How They’re Prepping for Thanksgiving
items.description: Food Network chefs Bobby Flay and Brooke Williamson are getting ready for another Thanksgiving celebration at their beautiful Hamptons home, and they've shared their best tips and tricks ahead of the holiday. In an interview with People magazine, the power couple said that their best advice is to start dinner prep early. “Prep as much as you can ahead of time,” said Williamson, 48. “I think stuffing tastes better the next day, once it’s had a chance to meld together.” Flay , 61, dropped another helpful piece of advice: “Have chicken stock on your stove. It reheats the sliced turkey, which ultimately gets dried out no matter what you do. It can also thin out gravy that gets too thick.” While one might assume that having two celebrity chefs in a household can feel like a case of too many cooks in the kitchen, the duo said it’s never a problem for them. Loading... Celebrity chefs Bobby Flay and Brooke Williamson are preparing to host a Tuscan-inspired Thanksgiving dinner. Winnie Au/PEOPLE Loading... The couple shared a look at the home kitchen of their New York City residence with People magazine. Winnie Au/PEOPLE Loading... Despite each having command of the kitchen, they say "it never feels like we're in each other's way." Winnie Au/PEOPLE “We definitely split up the work,” said Williamson. “It never feels like we’re in each other’s way. It feels like it makes sense.” Flay and Williamson invited the publication into the kitchen of their New York City home, showing off the gorgeous cabinets and generously sized island. After a recent trip to Italy , the couple told the magazine that they’re planning a Tuscan-inspired feast this year, joking that it’ll be a “mini ‘Brady Bunch’” scenario with their blended families. Flay is dad to 30-year-old Sophie , while Williamson has a son, Hudson , 18. In September, Flay spoke about the home kitchens he has in his two residences—his Tribeca pad and an estate in the Hamptons. “The kitchen is spacious, and I make three meals a day in there,” he told The Wall Street Journal . ”The space relaxes me and allows me to cook for family and friends.” In his home out East, the kitchen is not just a place to whip up delicious meals. The room functions more like a full-fledged restaurant. “On the other side of my sizable island are three French cafe tables for guests,” he explained. The setup is even equipped with a professional fryer, which he described as a “recent kitchen splurge.” Among his latest kitchen tools is a utensil he’s relied on for years: “I still have the chef’s knife I used at [the French Culinary Institute],” he shared. “When [I] prepare food with it, the feel reminds me that I’m still learning every day." The kitchen of the Amagansett home is his favorite place to cook and where he has typically hosted Thanksgiving. Loading... Flay recently gifted Williamson a gorgeous diamond ring to show his commitment without entering another marriage. Winnie Au/PEOPLE Flay built the dwelling from the ground up during his marriage to “Law and Order: SVU” actress Stephanie March . The former couple, who divorced in 2015, hosted a turkey dinner for a staggering 50 guests at their first Thanksgiving in the home. “I prepared two 30-pound turkeys and cooked sides for days,” he recalled in a 2013 interview with Elle Decor . “I stand at my kitchen island from the minute I get out here to the minute I leave.” Although Flay has publicly discussed his desire to steer clear of matrimony after three divorces, he and Williamson have agreed on an alternative way to show their commitment to each other. “She’s like, ‘I just want a big ring and a big party,’ and I was like, ‘I love that idea because my marriages have not lasted, unfortunately,’” he told People. Explaining that the “most important thing” is to “make sure that Brooke feels like she’s committed to,” he recalled of the moment he gifted her a “giant diamond ring” during a trip to London. Williamson describes the flashy piece of jewelry as “the perfect ring,” adding that “it’s very sparkly.” Although she was initially thrown off by the gesture, she now sports the rock on her right hand. “I thought it was incredibly thoughtful,” said Williamson. “He said just because I don’t feel the need to get married or want to get married again doesn’t mean that you don’t deserve the big, beautiful ring that comes along with it.” While Flay has been private about his past relationships, he admits he’s been more open this time around, and cites all they have in common for his “confidence” about their partnership. “I feel very confident about this,” he said of the pair’s connection. “There’s so many wonderful things about it.” Get real estate news in your inbox Sign up now Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

items.title: Mortgage rates fell and demand steadied as inventory dipped
items.description: Mortgage rates fell, demand stabilized and inventory had a noticeable decline last week. But are the changes in demand and inventory data about seasonality, or has the housing market changed with the recent mortgage rate decline? Let’s take a look at the weekend tracker and see what the data is telling us with rates falling the last three weeks. 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% What a crazy time in the bond market recently: the key level of 5.35% has not only held since early October, but the reversal has been truly nice to watch. The midterm elections , which changed the control of the House and Senate, have added another variable into the mortgage rate equation. I discussed what Congress can do to help lower mortgage rates on this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler, but for now the head-and-shoulders pattern of the 10-year yield is still somewhat intact, though a fight for it to break lower is happening. I wouldn’t get too excited about mortgage rates until the 10-year yield can break under 4.70% and have follow-through bond buying, but mortgage rates have fallen and demand has stabilized over the last few weeks. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multiyear lows. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% — spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility. That said, if mortgage spreads weren’t near multiyear lows right now, we'd have no chance of getting mortgage rates below 7.25%, and demand wouldn't have stabilized recently. Now that spreads have moved up from this year's lows, we can clearly see that mortgage rates would be sub-7% if spreads return to that level. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.27% from 2.23% a week earlier. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle. If we had the best levels of spreads in 2026, mortgage rates would be 6.72% today, not 7.17% . If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.11% today, not 7.17% . Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. The key for the last three weeks: lower rates, even above 7%, have stabilized demand, as our weekly pending sales have shown. Now, this isn’t growth, just stabilization from a noticeable slowdown when mortgage rates got toward 7.60%. The last three years and 10 months show that housing demand grows when mortgage rates fall below 6.64% and head toward 6%; above 7%, we don’t have much growth data beyond seasonal demand. Last year at this time, mortgage rates were headed toward 6%, so the year-over-year comps will be hard for some time. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 51,764 2025: 59,164 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. We had a small decline week to week; I can see the stabilization here as well and the year-over-year comps will also be very difficult here, as last year at this time rates were heading toward 6%. Earlier in the year, when rates were lower, pretty much every week this year showed growth. Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026: 16 positive week-to-week prints 24 negative week-to-week prints 5 flat week-to-week prints 10 weeks of double-digit year-over-year growth 25 weeks of positive year-over-year growth 15 negative year-over-year prints Housing inventory Housing inventory growth has been very tame this year, with some weeks being down year over year. However, when mortgage rates got above 6.64% and then headed toward 7.60%, we did see some growth pick up. Also, rates were lower last year so demand was heading toward a nine-month high in December, which means it the comps will be easier to show growth in inventory. Inventory growth is running at 7.18% even with easier comps. Weekly inventory change (Oct. 30-Nov. 6): Inventory fell from 914,833 to 902,740 Same week last year (Oct. 31-Nov 7): Inventory fell from 856,751 to 842,257 New listings New listings are in their typical seasonal decline; 2026 has been the healthiest new-listings year since 2022, with over 80,000 new listings per week a few times this year. The concern I had was that if higher rates cause sellers to stop listing their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 — that would hurt supply and demand. However, that hasn’t happened in any meaningful way. Most home sellers are buyers, and now that rates have fallen a smidge, it looks like we can end the year on a positive note for 2026 for new listings. In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years . Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years: 2026: 54,479 2025: 55,486 Price-cut percentage Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%; demand fell, and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%. items.title: Why didn’t the strong jobs report send mortgage rates skyrocketing?
items.description: With all the crazy things happening this week, the blowout jobs report on Friday didn’t send mortgage rates up at all. But one thing is for sure: the labor market has been better in 2026 than it was in 2025. I once labelled the labor market the honey badger labor market and no matter what has been thrown at the U.S. economy after 2011 — outside the brief recession created by COVID-19 — the labor data has held up well. Let’s dig into why very strong jobs report didn’t push yields or mortgage rates higher, as we would normally expect with the Fed being so hawkish in their statement. From BLS : Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. The labor data has improved enough that we have gone from a 4.5% unemployment rate last year to 4.1% today. Part of this is that labor-force growth has slowed and the break-even number has decreased, meaning fewer jobs are needed to keep the unemployment rate low. I have my break-even at 78,000 jobs created per month; I believe the Fed's is 33,000. Some economists have it at zero, which I think is silly. In any case, the unemployment rate is lower this year versus last year. Now, the low point in the COVID-19 recovery was about 3.4% unemployment back in 2023, so the unemployment rate has increased from that low, but it's still good enough to keep the Fed’s focus on inflation instead of labor. Jobs breakdown This month's report had growth in a few sectors, especially the business services sector jobs with one of the biggest monthly prints in years. There was also growth in manufacturing, and transportation & warehouse, while construction jobs faded a tad. Construction labor will be interesting in the future if mortgage rates stay elevated and short-term rates go up. If there is an AI slowdown and fewer AI data centers are being built, will this sector start to decline? One of my most critical recession indicators, residential construction employment, doesn’t look great lately, but it isn’t looking terrible either. In previous cycles, you can see a clear downtrend in this labor pool, which hasn’t happened in this cycle. With builders doing more rate buydowns — which have kept new home sales at 2019 levels over the past few years — and remodeling work holding up, this clear recession indicator hasn’t broken yet. 10-year yield and mortgage rates As crazy as this week has been, the jobs data wasn’t the big driver of mortgage rates as much as AI stock prices. CoreWeave's stock price was up 10% pre-market today, and bond yields ticked up with that. The jobs report didn’t do much to yields, we just saw a mild increase and then they fell back in line with the trend. Then CoreWeave stock price went almost negative, bond yields fell to the lows of the day, and now both have picked up from the lows! The market needs a weekend break. Mortgage rates ended the day flat at 7.17%, so as crazy as this sounds, the blowout jobs data didn’t send mortgage rates or bond yields much higher. That's good news for rates, and there are some levers the new Congress can pull to potentially get rates even lower, which I discussed on today's episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler. Conclusion A lot has changed this week for the economy regarding the bond market and where mortgage rates can go. The blue wave has raised hopes that the trade war and the conflict with Iran can end soon, AI companies have shown they can bleed, and Congress will try to slow the AI boom as much as it can without crashing it. All these things happened this week, so that even with four solid jobs reports during jobs week, the 10-year yield closed at 4.86% and mortgage rates closed at weekly lows. Related More: Jobs Report

items.title: Opendoor says it's behind schedule but plans to catch up by 2027
items.description: Opendoor is behind schedule. Since taking over the company a little over a year ago, CEO Kaz Nejatian has promised that the firm would achieve adjusted net income positive status on a 12-month go-forward basis by the end of 2026. But the recent housing market downturn, triggered by the rapid rise in mortgage rates , has proven to be a bit of a roadblock. “We are currently behind but we intend to catch up,” the iBuyer’s third quarter 2026 earnings report explained. During the quarter, Opendoor recorded an adjusted net loss of $66 million and an actual net loss of $218 million, up from a $90 million net loss a year ago. This comes even as the company reported a 12% annual increase in revenue to $1.022 billion. “A year ago, I told you we would build a different Opendoor — faster, stronger, fully committed to our mission of tilting the world in favor of homeowners,” Nejatian said during his firm’s earnings call with investors and analysts on Thursday. “We have spent the past year building a machine, and that machine is getting better every single day. We are not done yet. It is not perfect, but it is getting better every single day. The question is this: Is Opendoor in a better economic condition than it was a year ago? The answer is obviously yes.” A more resilient Opendoor Nejatian’s confidence comes from his belief that Opendoor has become more resilient over the past year. This includes ways in which the company has worked to serve more sellers without adding more homes to the company’s balance sheet. “This past week, around half of the first offers our direct-to-consumer sellers accepted were listing or Cash Now, More Later. That lets us serve more sellers with less of our capital exposed to changes in the market,” Nejatian said. In the past 12 months, the company has done over $1 billion in Cash Now, More Later volume. “We have built more ways to meet sellers' needs and have made it easier for them to understand their options and make the choice they want for their own lives,” Nejatian said. “Sellers can now adjust the offer slides and make the choice that is good for their families.” Scaling without buying more homes? Nejatian noted that every other time Opendoor has tried to scale, it has done so by purchasing more properties, but that isn’t the case this time. “We proved that we can grow without buying growth. That's the single most important thing that has happened over the last year. We're changing that with our capital-light products,” Nejatian said. Still, Opendoor did purchase far more homes in Q3 2026 than it did in Q3 2025, with a 316% year-over-year increase to 4,865 homes. The company’s signed acquisition volume represented an estimated 0.56% of market share in the addressable U.S. market in Q3 2026 — more than four times higher than a year ago. On the sales side, Opendoor sold 2,728 homes, an increase of 160 homes compared to a year ago. At the end of the quarter, the iBuyer had 7,596 homes in its inventory, up from 3,139 homes a year ago. While the increase in inventory could be seen as cause for concern, especially heading into the slower winter housing market, Opendoor noted that homes listed for sale for 120 days represented just 18% of inventory at the end of the quarter, down from 50% a year ago. Despite the progress, Nejatian said the company still has work left to do on unit economics and resale velocity, something it needs to focus on as it strives for more resiliency. “We're not as good as we want to be, but we're in a much better place," he said. "When the market moves against you and you own homes, there's two things you can do. You can sell fast, or you can hold and wait and pray for the market to recover. We choose to clear. "The decline in late August and September knocked us off track on execution a little bit because we turned our attention to clearance rather than margin improvement. It costs something real in a quarter like this, but that's the right way to run this company for the long run.” To help with some of these challenges, Nejatian said Opendoor has turned to AI to help improve speed while still scaling. Some of these tools include an AI model that determines repair plans for every home to hit the market. The company said the system has been outperforming the old process of following a standard repair manual. Opendoor said it also built a system to help price homes. While humans still have final judgment, the software does the work of pulling applicable, comparable homes. Ancillary services and the future Nejatian also said that Opendoor is focusing on its mortgage division . In Q3, Opendoor said originations from its in-house lender were up 400% year over year. This comes as the iBuyer's lender is now licensed in 25 states, compared to none a year ago. In addition, the company also launched a beta test of Buy with Opendoor in the San Francisco Bay Area this week. The product allows the company to earn mortgage revenue on properties not affiliated with Opendoor in anyway. Looking to the future, Nejatian said Opendoor is hoping to build out title and escrow services — not only to add more efficiencies to Opendoor’s in-house transactions but to add additional revenue streams by serving consumers not in its ecosystem. “We need to grow, use less capital per transaction, and sell homes faster. Those are things we can control, and that is what we are focused on. What matters to us is solving the core problems of our business, and those are what we need to focus on,” Nejatian said. items.title: Progress Residential to pay $49.8M to settle FTC, state claims over rental practices
items.description: Progress Residential , the property manager of single-family rental homes owned by Pretium Partners , has agreed to pay $49.8 million to settle deceptive and unfair practices claims by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and state regulators. The company denies any wrongdoing. In a complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia , regulators alleged that the company advertised rental prices that did not reflect the full amount tenants would be required to pay, imposed hidden or inadequately disclosed fees and charges, and mishandled security deposits. The claims also included that Progress misrepresented the condition and move-in readiness of properties, restricted tenants’ ability to share reviews, and failed to adequately address tenant complaints and maintenance issues. In a statement given to HousingWire , a representative of Progress Residential and Pretium said the companies have reached an agreement “with the FTC and four states to resolve the Commission’s Civil Investigative Demand related to certain aspects of our resident experience during the period of 2021 to 2025.” “The agreement contains no admission of wrongdoing, and we maintain Progress’ practices have been transparent, fair, and consistent with industry practice,” the spokesperson said. “Although we disagree with the FTC’s claims, this resolution allows us to move forward with our mission of expanding access to quality, affordable rental housing in neighborhoods of opportunity.” The deal was reached by the FTC, the attorneys general of Arizona, Indiana and Colorado, and the Utah Division of Consumer Protection . It combines monetary relief for renters across the country. “We will always welcome investment in housing and recognize the important role private capital can play in increasing opportunities for Hoosier families,” Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said in a statement. “But no company, regardless of size or financial backing, gets a free pass to mislead consumers, impose hidden charges or treat tenants unfairly.” “Consumers searching for housing should have access to straightforward information about the costs associated with renting a home,” said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “Transparency regarding rental prices and fees helps consumers compare options and make informed choices. Clear pricing practices also support competition by allowing housing providers to compete on the basis of price, quality and service. "The FTC is monitoring the rental housing market and will continue to take action where appropriate to ensure that consumers receive clear and accurate information about the costs of renting a home.” Per the settlement terms, Progress must disclose the total monthly rental price in advertisements and listings, along with mandatory fees and charges, before a consumer commits to rent. The company also must stop withholding funds for ordinary wear and tear and is prohibited from misleading claims about property conditions. The consumer redress funds created by the settlement total $48.5 million and will be used for relief as directed by the stipulated order entered in the federal case. Arizona is receiving $1.25 million. In 2024, Invitation Homes , the largest owner of U.S. single-family rental homes, agreed to pay $48 million to consumers and change some of its practices. items.title: 220-Unit Mixed-Use Project Moves Forward Near Rowan University
items.description: Hundreds of new apartments have been approved on a former industrial site in the center of a South Jersey college town. Google Maps 220 Rowan Blvd., another Nexus Properties project in Glassboro The Glassboro Planning Board voted Wednesday to greenlight Nexus Properties ’ plans for 220 units and about 8K SF of retail on the corner of Academy and East High streets in the town's central business district, 42Freeway reported . The market-rate project, dubbed Glassworks, will span two city blocks and six stories on a site about three-quarters of a mile from the core of Rowan University’s campus. Nexus expects the project to deliver sometime in 2029, 70and73 reported . Its new retail component will effectively be a replacement for older commercial properties that existed on the site. The site once housed the Whitney Glass Works, which closed in the 1920s. The Heritage Glass Museum operates in the neighborhood and will remain open, alongside Angelo’s Diner. The former Glassboro Library is set to be razed. Lawrenceville-based Nexus is also a major student housing owner in Glassboro, with five properties listed on its website. Some of those are part of the Rowan Boulevard project, where Nexus struck up a $425M public-private partnership with Rowan University to build a mixed-use neighborhood overlooking the campus. While permitting can be a challenge in South Jersey, the region is seeing some multifamily development, a large share of which is affordable housing meant to meet state requirements for municipalities under the Mount Laurel doctrine. Enforcement of the 1975 New Jersey Supreme Court decision requiring local governments to use zoning to further attainable housing production was clarified in 2024. That push is also underway in Voorhees, where 180 affordable units are on the way. Administrators there greenlit plans for a 178-unit, market-rate office-to-residential conversion last month. But mixed-use plans for a redevelopment of the nearby Echelon Mall have fallen through since they were introduced last year, the Philadelphia Business Journal reported this week. Hoboken Brownstone Co . told the outlet this was due to uncertainty about a $90M tax credit it sought through New Jersey’s Aspire program, which has paused its application process.
