items.title: NYC Claims Nearly Half Of State's Opportunity Zones, Putting New Neighborhoods In Play
items.description: The opportunity zone guessing game is over. On Thursday, the Treasury Department released the official list of census tracts eligible for the federal tax incentive program's second iteration, giving investors sitting in Park Avenue towers a new map to pore over. Pexels/Raphael Loquellano Brooklyn’s Bedford-Stuyvesant is among the neighborhoods designated as opportunity zones. “About $100B was deployed in the last decade to the program, probably half of that was quote-unquote institutional capital,” Ackman-Ziff Real Estate Group Director Andrew Rudy said. “I wouldn't be surprised if there was a doubling of capital formation for this iteration of the law versus the last.” Leading up to the release, New York was among the few states to publicize little information about the process. Stricter requirements for census tracts qualifying as “economically distressed” and Congress’ aim of funneling more money toward rural areas raised concerns over which New York City neighborhoods would be selected. The final deadline for states to submit their opportunity zone nominations was Oct. 28, after which Treasury reviewed them before releasing the full list. New York ultimately had 430 census tracts designated as opportunity zones, 210 of which are in the five boroughs. Brooklyn and the Bronx received the greatest number of designations, with 67 and 57, respectively. Another 41 are in Manhattan , 35 are in Queens and 10 are on Staten Island . The program allows investors to defer capital gains taxes and lower the basis on which they are taxed by investing in real estate projects or businesses that spur economic growth in select low-income communities. OZ 1.0, created under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 , used 2010 census data, allowing several neighborhoods already booming with development to qualify. It also gave benefits to projects in tracts adjacent to qualifying zones — a loophole that was removed from 2.0 — further drawing investment to highly developed neighborhoods. Because OZ 2.0 is based on the 2020 census, many areas that benefited the most under the program’s predecessor no longer qualify. Still, New York City’s density, alongside public housing developments and rent-stabilized units, means that some neighborhoods that don’t seem blighted qualify under the poverty threshold. The new map includes parts of Manhattan’s Lower East Side , Harlem and the Upper West Side , but the more appealing sites may be in areas where developers can layer subsidies, according to Ackman-Ziff Director Jordan Brustein. “For example, Yonkers , which is a more emerging area, is still well located on the transportation line and near the city. Developers are able to get unique incentives that yield better returns, which ultimately end up attracting more equity,” Brustein said. “So to us, we're more interested there than maybe even some of these better-located assets that have thinner return profiles.” Prized areas of the outer boroughs include Brooklyn’s Bedford-Stuyvesant , which has become increasingly gentrified, and areas of the East Bronx near the Metro-North’s station expansion. Queens’ Sunnyside Yards , where Mayor Zohran Mamdani is seeking to advance a 12,000-unit residential development , also received designation, despite not being on the initial list of eligible tracts. It is only one of two tracts nationwide to do so, with the other being in Hawaii. But unlike rural areas of the country, where the primary issue for development is attracting capital interest, New York City developers struggle with policies that make building more difficult. Under 485-x , higher construction wage requirements kick in for larger housing projects. As a result, the vast majority of proposals filed in the last two years are for buildings with 99 units or less. Rudy and Brustein said many investors are gravitating toward shovel-ready sites eligible under 1.0 as they raise capital for 2.0. Despite stronger markets like Long Island City no longer being included, the two-year transition period allows developers to continue accepting funds. Faced with higher interest rates and stricter lending standards , some developers in OZ 1.0 zones have pushed through the predevelopment process only to stall out before getting shovels in the ground. As long as they’ve followed compliance, those projects are likely to be among the first to be injected with OZ 2.0 funds. “Think about it this way: There’s a reason why they’re not in 2.0 maps,” Brustein said. “The capital markets have been challenging, and the one bright spot right now in the market is opportunity zones .” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Ackman-Ziff Real Estate Group , Brooklyn , Manhattan , Opportunity zones , opportunity zones 2.0 , Queens , Staten Island , Sunnyside Yards , The Bronx

items.title: Centennial Shopping Center Sells For $31M: The Denver Deal Sheet
items.description: Courtesy of Continental Realty Corp. Quebec Village Shopping Center at 8223 S. Quebec St. in Centennial A 125K SF shopping center in Centennial sold to an out-of-state investment and management company on Thursday. Baltimore, Maryland-based Continental Realty Corp . purchased Quebec Village Shopping Center, at 8223 S. Quebec St., from Kensington Development Partners . CRC purchased the shopping center at a “significant discount to replacement cost,” CRC co-Chief Investment Officer Josh Dinstein said in a statement. Quebec Village Shopping Center was built in 1988. Its tenants include Chase Bank, Starbucks, Golf Haus, Subway, Great Clips and GNC. Amazon also leases 43K SF at the center for a planned Amazon Fresh grocery store that never opened . This is CRC’s second retail center purchase in the Denver metro. The company acquired the 266K SF Thornton Town Center for $25.5M in late 2025. CRC has acquired about $1B worth of real estate since early 2021, the company said in a statement. The company, founded in 1960, specializes in acquiring and managing retail and multifamily properties. CBRE represented Illinois-based Kensington Development Partners. PEOPLE Denver Urban Renewal Authority named a new executive director. Kenneth Ho will take over the role on Dec. 1. He has more than 25 years of experience in urban planning and real estate development and investment. Ho previously worked as chief operating officer at Fitzsimons Innovation Community. SALES Courtesy of Cushman & Wakefield Lamar Station Plaza is home to Casa Bonita. items.title: GSE delinquencies climb: Don't shift staff solely to FHA
items.description: GSE delinquencies climb: Don't shift staff solely to FHA By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published November 06, 2026, 4:11 p.m. EST | Updated November 06, 2026, 5:21 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: Whether mortgage servicers can maintain enough resources to handle rising agency loan distress Supporting Data: 6.9%: The late-summer increase in short-term delinquent GSE-backed mortgages. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. A late-summer rise in delinquencies among mortgages backed by the government-sponsored enterprises points to an upward trend that may require servicers to keep resources available for agency loans until economic conditions improve. Processing Content Delinquency totals increased on a month-to-month basis across stages in August, according to data provided by the Federal Housing Finance Agency, the overseer of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. The number of borrowers 30 to 59 days delinquent climbed 6.9% to 313,254 from 292,965 between July and August . The number of mortgages past due by 60 days or more grew 2.9% to 256,999 units compared to 249,816 one month earlier. The representative share of delinquencies relative to all outstanding GSE-backed mortgages now stands at 1.03% for early-stage distress. Liens 60 to 90 days past due make up 0.84% of outstanding mortgages. Borrowers in serious delinquency or currently in foreclosure account for 0.6%. Although mortgage leaders in 2026 raised regular warnings about looming challenges for borrowers with Federal Housing Administration mortgages , the new data hints at difficulties surfacing in the agency segment. While distress eased in the early summer, delinquency volumes finished August higher than where they stood at the end of the first quarter, when they settled at 281,098 and 246,081, respectively. FHFA's findings suggest rising prices and economic uncertainty continue to take a significant toll on the ability of some homeowners to consistently meet monthly mortgage obligations, with downward pressure on affordability becoming more acute as 2026 progresses. The surge in summer delinquencies came at the same time prices of consumer goods ticked upward, with energy costs, in particular, accelerating from the impact of the Iran War. Meanwhile, the still-rising costs of property insurance and taxes are leading to prolonged sticker shock, even as the pace appears to be leveling off this year. Recent forecasts predict many of the same factors will weigh on affordability through next year. The extent of homeowner concerns showed up in the number of calls for legal assistance to deal with potential foreclosures in the late summer, which came in almost 15% higher at the end of the third quarter compared to a year ago. Lawyers at LegalShield specifically noted inflation's effect on household budgets as a primary cause , rather than poor planning on the part of borrowers. Foreclosure starts leap 18% FHFA's new report also found foreclosures on the rise among Fannie Mae- and Freddie Mac-backed loans. The number of foreclosure starts shot up 18% to 8,930 from 7,569 from July to August. Foreclosure and bank sales of properties eased 5%, though, to 1,333 from 1,403. A report from Auction.com saw such inventory likely to increase for the remainder of 2026, but much of the growth will be driven by FHA foreclosures. The FHFA also recorded 7,675 permanent loan modifications in August, increasing from 7,503 a month earlier. More than one-third, or 36.5%, of modifications involved extending the term of payment. In total, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac completed 16,335 actions in August aimed at foreclosure prevention. items.title: Lenders turn to cuts, AI as strong jobs point to rate hikes
items.description: Lenders turn to cuts, AI as strong jobs point to rate hikes By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published November 06, 2026, 1:38 p.m. EST | Updated November 06, 2026, 3:35 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Discover why nonbank mortgage payrolls hit a 2026 low despite rising retail productivity gains. Expert Quote: "For housing, stronger hiring cuts both ways." — Sam Williamson, Senior Economist, First American. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Nonbank mortgage payroll estimates dropped to a low for 2026 ahead of broader employment gains last month, pointing to a persistent need to manage origination staffing with retail productivity initiatives that have not yet reduced costs but at least contained them. Processing Content Industry-specific data the Bureau of Labor Statistics released with a one-month lag for real-estate credit and loan brokers, when combined, show industry payrolls dropped to 265,100 in August, marking the lowest point since the seasonally-slow first quarter. The statistics, combined with October's strong jobs report signaling a likelihood rates won't immediately fall further , suggest the industry is reducing origination staffing but are able to do so gradually as artificial intelligence has helped boost the number of loans closers handle. "There are a lot of learnings that can happen in this tighter market,'" Walter Mullen, chief strategy officer at Onity , said at IMN's mortgage servicing rights conference this week, noting that origination declines have forced companies to broadly explore operational innovation. Where retail fulfillment productivity stands The number of loans handled by full-time equivalent employees in retail fulfillment have inched up this year primarily due to a surge in closer gains, according to data the Mortgage Bankers Association and Stratmor Group have collected from lenders. The average monthly number of loans per closer jumped from 36.7 to 41.5 between 2025 and 2026 while lenders reported a far more modest gain for processors and a slight decline in productivity in underwriting in line with the more challenging origination environment. Lenders reported a mix of artificial intelligence and leaner staffing drove the productivity gains, which did not reduce costs but have prevented them from rising. Current employment trends: A mixed blessing While the latest industry-specific and total job numbers point to some challenges for mortgage companies, housing economists noted they do point to some offsetting positives for lenders too. "For housing, stronger hiring cuts both ways. More jobs mean more income and more reasons to move, while a stronger economy could prolong the wait for mortgage-rate relief," Sam Williamson, senior economist at First American, wrote in an emailed press statement. October's stronger-than-anticipated gain of 165,000 and a decline in the unemployment rate from 4.2% to 4.1% came with wage gains, according to Williamson. However, MBA noted that there also were indications in the numbers that some workers are underemployed. "While the headline unemployment rate decreased, some of this was due to individuals taking part-time work when they would have preferred a full-time position," MBA Chief Economist Mike Fratantoni wrote in his emailed statement. Despite some signs of weakness like this, Frantantoni said he still anticipates that the overall impact of the numbers will be an increased likelihood that the Federal Open Market Committee will raise short-term rates at one of two of its next meetings. "A resilient job market, combined with inflation that is still too high, is likely to lead the FOMC to hike rates in December. MBA anticipates another hike as well in the first quarter of 2027," he said. While the short-term rates the Fed controls have some bearing on long-term mortgage rates that currently dominate the housing market, mortgage spreads also drive the cost of funds for homebuyers. items.title: Zillow's agent tie-ins grab purchase share as market shrinks
items.description: Zillow's agent tie-ins grab purchase share as market shrinks By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 05, 2026, 4:39 p.m. EST | Updated November 05, 2026, 4:45 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Zillow's strategy of pairing its loan officers with invitation-only real estate agents is pulling purchase business away from the rest of the market. Its home loans unit grew purchase volume 55% in the third quarter while industry purchase originations fell. Processing Content Zillow Home Loans originated $1.972 billion of purchase loans in the third quarter, up from $1.276 billion a year earlier. Year-to-date volume is up 79%. Over the same quarter, Zillow estimates industry purchase origination volume declined 4%. "It's why purchase mortgage revenue for us is outgrowing the category even with the category declining," said CEO Jeremy Wacksman on the earnings call. The company is almost entirely a purchase lender. It did just $4 million of refinance production in the third quarter, versus $5 million one year prior. Second quarter volume was $2.181 billion, with only $7 million coming from refi. How the Preferred program feeds Zillow Home Loans The volume growth came as Zillow expanded the share of buyer connections sent through its Preferred program, an invitation-only network of real estate agents. Zillow previously called the program Flex. Executives reported double-digit adoption of Zillow Home Loans among customers working with Preferred agents. In Zillow's oldest markets, that rate is approximately 20%. "We are pleased that we continue to see double-digit customer adoption rates in Zillow Home Loans with our oldest markets at approximately 20% adoption rates, demonstrating that our integrated experience is adding value for both consumers and real estate agents," said Jeremy Hoffman, chief operating and chief financial officer. Wacksman framed the integrated model as the reason for Zillow's confidence in mortgage growth. "I mean 80% of buyers need both the mortgage and the agent. They want that as a one-stop shop," he said. "When we can offer that as an integrated experience, that's what they're choosing." He added that "a key part of this strategy is making sure that the Home Loans loan officer and the Preferred agent build a mutually beneficial relationship." The shift also changes how Zillow gets paid. Under its legacy advertising model, real estate agents used co-marketing dollars from lenders when bidding on leads, said Douglas Harter of BTIG. Under the Preferred model, Zillow captures mortgage revenue at origination, which can come six to 12 months later. Why mortgage revenue still missed The volume gains did not translate into the revenue analysts expected. Mortgage revenue rose 32% year-over-year to $70 million, but Keefe, Bruyette & Woods had forecast $81.3 million, putting the result 13.9% short. BTIG had forecast $81 million. Hoffman attributed the miss to " rate shock , which caused lower conversions." Industry purchase volume also came in weaker than Zillow planned for. "We estimate that industry mortgage purchase origination volumes were down 4% for Q3, below our expectation for a low-single-digit decline," he said. "We call out mortgage industry performance because the majority of Zillow buyers purchased their home with a mortgage." Harter tied the broader earnings miss to a weakening housing market and the "accelerated transition from the legacy ad model to Flex." Zillow underperformed existing home sales for the first time since the fourth quarter of 2024, which helped spread the miss into mortgage, he said in a research note. Zillow posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, compared with $10 million of net income in the third quarter of 2025. Zillow expects a steeper purchase decline in Q4 Zillow guided fourth quarter mortgage revenue to between $55 million and $56 million, with total revenue between $635 million and $665 million. "Our revenue outlook includes our expectation for a decline in year-over-year mortgage industry purchase origination volumes of 10% to 15%," Hoffman said. "This is down significantly from our prior industry expectation of mid-single-digits decline due to the sharp increase in mortgage rates we saw at the end of Q3 and into the start of Q4." Zillow expects 20% revenue growth in the fourth quarter as it scales outside its residential business, "with mortgage tailing off," Harter said. "The weakening housing market and bigger-than-anticipated model transition impact contributed to an 8-9% reduction in the 4Q revenue guide from the prior implied level," he said. "Headwinds are expected to carry into '27." Brad Finkelstein Originations Editor Brad Finkelstein is the originations editor of National Mortgage News. items.title: Two Neighboring $9.9 Million Oceanfront Homes Just Listed in Kauai’s South Shore—And They Can Form an Ultra-Luxe Compound
items.description: Tucked into a private-club community in Hawaii called Kukui‘ula , two luxury homes just hit the market on Kauai's South Shore . Set right on the ocean, and set among lush tropical vegetation, this walkable community is only 25-minute drive from Lihue Airport. "The close proximity of everything is very convenient. You’re not having to spend a lot of time in the car,” says Pancho Sullivan of Hawaii Life , who is co-listing the two homes with Haunani Sullivan as well as Suzanne Harding and Jeff Skinner of Kukui‘ula Realty Group . The asking price sits at $9,900,000 each. Both were built in 2025 and have never been occupied. Aepo Nei 18 and Aepo Nei 19 are neighboring 3,372-square-foot homes with four bedrooms and 4.5 baths each. They can be purchased together, to create a private compound, or by separate buyers. Even better, the homes are fully furnished and stocked with items like bed and bath linens, beach towels, and everything you need to cook and serve in the kitchen, such as bowls, plates and glasses. Loading... Aepo Nei 18’s layout features connected pavilions. Steven Lippman / homesbystevenlippman.com Loading... The homes both feature 180-degree ocean views. Steven Lippman / homesbystevenlippman.com Loading... The homes feature lush living areas. Loading... The homes were constructed with natural materials like lava stone, coral and teak. Steven Lippman / homesbystevenlippman.com But it’s the design by Brazil-based Architects+CO that’s truly unique. Kauai Bahia Construction and their in-house material company, Kayu, handled all of the finish material production and millwork installation. "Brazil is known for incredible resort-club communities," says Pancho. "We actually traveled to Brazil to look at some of the clubs they designed. It’s the same tropical feel (as Hawaii) that blends in really well with nature." Aepo Nei 18’s layout features connected pavilions while Aepo Nei 19’s living spaces open onto a lawn courtyard. Design features at both include deep roof overhangs, walls of glass and multiple outdoor living spaces such as an infinity-edge pool; jacuzzi; swim-in, swim-out sauna; and in-water fire pit. "They both have beautiful 180-degree ocean views looking across the Tom Weiskopf -designed golf course. The swim-in, swim-out dry sauna facing the ocean is a unique feature," says Pancho, adding that the usage of natural materials like lava stone, coral and teak "fit into the landscape very beautifully." Referred to as the Garden Island, Kauai is home to about 73,000 people. "We get the majority of the island’s sunshine down here," says Haunani, about the South Shore. "People flock here for the beaches and the sunshine, Hawaiian monk seals on the sand, and a lot of ocean activity including surfing. "A lot of people that venture to Kauai are adventure seekers. We have great hiking. You can get on a boat and dive on the Nā Pali Coast and do ziplining and ATV tours." Loading... The exterior Aepo Nei 19’, which features deep roof overhangs. Steven Lippman / homesbystevenlippman.com Loading... One of the bathrooms, with natural features. Loading... Both homes come fully furnished. Stand-up paddleboarding, diving and fishing are two other activities easy to do in this community. Homeowners become club members with access to dining, a pool, spa (boasting a steam rook and lava-rock dry sauna), pickleball and tennis courts, and an 18-hole golf course. "There’s an incredible gym with classes daily, from yoga to sound bathing to fitness training," says Pancho. "All of that is part of your club membership. It’s a great place to be in tune with nature and get healthy." A 10-acre organic garden features a farm stand as well as opportunities to create floral bouquets. There’s also a conscious effort to honor Hawaiian history through cultural-heritage walks; sunrise ceremonies; hula performances; and classes in Hawaiian featherwork, quilting and basket weaving. “Members who are part of the club become life-long friends,” says Haunani. “They’re going to each other’s second homes and weddings. They travel around the world together.” The community also organizes annual golf and pickleball tournaments for members, and three golf courses are within a seven-minute drive. Loading... Like it's neighbor, the home features 180-degree ocean views. Loading... The living areas open onto an open courtyard and pool area. items.title: Meet the 27-Year-Old Who’s Trying To Bring Housing Back to Rural Ohio
items.description: When it comes to the hottest locations that attract young 20-somethings, Mansfield, OH , probably isn't the first place that comes to mind. For years, Mansfield’s nickname was “The Fun Center of Ohio ” because of its family-friendly attractions and its status in the 1970s as a mini-bike manufacturing hub. More recently, the town of 47,000, located halfway between Columbus and Cleveland , earned the local nickname of “Danger City” after the Westinghouse electric plant left in 1990 and the town fell into deep economic decline. That didn’t stop Ben Goehner . The 27-year-old serial entrepreneur, who started a painting and landscaping business as a teenager, relocated to Mansfield from Seattle a year ago, hoping to revitalize rural housing through his vertically integrated housing development company, Western Dominion Land . Vertical integration is a development model in which a single company controls the full life cycle of a housing project. “In other countries, they’ve figured out that vertically integrating construction means you’re not paying a margin out to every single step," Goehner explains. "If you own the system—from a lumberyard, to producing panels or modular, to buying the land, to developing the land, to building the homes—you're not paying everyone’s markup along the way, and you can actually deliver that home at a reasonable price.” Goehner is building a factory in Mansfield to produce structured panels that he says will cut single-family home construction from months to weeks and allow him to charge much less than other builders. The first panels are expected to roll off the production line in early 2027. Currently, it takes 8.8 months to construct a home from start to finish, according to the National Association of Home Builders . Goehner says his process allows a home to be built and move-in-ready in 40 days. Western Dominion has already built about 500 housing units across Ohio, starting at $200,000 for a single-family home. Western Dominion focuses on what it calls "attainable housing"—homes priced below what the median household income in the area can afford but not income-limited, meaning they work for the vast majority of families and buyers. In Mansfield, where the median listing price is $229,000, he says, "single-family homes at $215,000 sold instantly. At $260,000, they sat for months." Loading... Ben Goehner says rural housing development has been sorely overlooked by large-scale developers. Ben Goehner As he sees it, 25% of the homes on the market are priced for 60% to 70% of buyers, while the rest of what’s being built is at the top end of the market. Furthermore, only 8% of construction happens in rural areas, despite 20% of the population living there. "The government is too focused on low-income housing" and low-income housing tax credits, he says. “And the last few housing bills they passed were only structured to deliver essentially more urban multifamily units and incentivize builders to build more low-income housing with tax credits." In rural communities, he adds, “We have a terrible amount of aged housing inventory. Most of our homes are from before 1970, which would be fine if it didn't cost so much to remodel. “From the '90s to the 2000s, we’re building a good amount of homes. As a country, we were doing about 1.6 million a year. And then in rural America, we were doing about 220,000 homes a year. And then 2008 hits, and that drops down to about 60,000 homes a year in rural America." Along the way, smaller builders disappeared, and larger builders were disincentivized from building in rural areas because of the red tape involved. "If you want to build in rural America and you go to a bank, unless you have all the cash, you have to show comps," he says. "You've got to be, like, ‘All right, we think these homes are going to sell for this much because these guys sold for this much.' And if no one's built for five to 50 years, which is the case in a lot of these communities, that can be difficult." The added costs of building in rural areas, like having to pull utilities, "mean you're spending $25,000 to $50,000 per lot before you can even start putting a house on it or connecting your utilities to the lot." Since the COVID-19 pandemic, home prices in rural communities have risen sharply. A Realtor.com® housing analysis of home prices from November 2019 to November 2025 found that median listing prices increased more than 70% in rural counties while in-metro counties saw home prices increase around 30% during the same time period. "A lot of the politicians we talk to, they go, 'I didn't know that that county needed housing. I didn't know rural needed housing because the population is shrinking.' But then when you look at why the population is shrinking, it's because they haven't gotten any new homes for 20 to 40 years." "You've got this huge demand. But on paper, on the surface, it looks like there's no demand because the population's declining," he continues. "And that's how you get cities like Holiday City." Loading... One of Western Dominion's attainable properties Western Dominion Land Co. Holiday City , near the Ohio border with Indiana and Michigan , has a population of just 48 people, but it is home to three large businesses—Chase Brass & Copper Co., 20/20 Custom Molded Products, and a Menards Distribution Center—which draw around 1,500 commuters from out of state. "Let's put up, you know, 300 homes, and a portion of the workforce can actually stop commuting an hour or two every day," Goehner says. Goehner hopes Ohio's new slate of elected officials will help advance rural building by offsetting some of the infrastructure-related costs of building in rural areas. In exchange, he would sell homes at his “attainable” housing rates. "The government needs to stop spending thousands of dollars a month per unit to subsidize rents when they could simply spend a little bit upfront to make it viable to build at a reasonable price point again," he says. items.title: Camden lowers guidance after September concession resurgence
items.description: Camden lowers guidance after September concession resurgence The REIT still saw improvement in expenses and new lease growth in Q3, though rising interest rates forced it to cancel property and land acquisitions. Published Nov. 6, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Wall Street sign with american flags and New York Stock Exchange in Manhattan, New York City, USA. Getty Images Camden’s Property Trust lowered its 2026 same-store revenue midpoint by 50 basis points to 0% after a weaker-than-expected September and the expectation of greater seasonal decline in the fourth quarter, according to the REIT’s executives on Friday’s third-quarter earnings call. Performance in September, specifically, surprised the company and set the stage for that revision, according to CEO Alex Jessett. “It was a greater decline in traffic than we had expected,” Jessett said. “And when we had the decline in traffic, obviously, you have to reduce your prices if you're trying to increase traffic.” Jessett said concessions, which were “incredibly sticky,” ranged from three weeks in West Palm Beach, Florida, up to two months in Austin, Texas, as merchant builders continued to offer steep discounts. “The third quarter, at least July and August, were so strong that we would have expected to see others start to dial back their concessions, and they absolutely did not do it,” Jessett said. Despite the September slowdown, there were positives: Camden expects same-store YOY expense growth of 1.75%, which is 75 bps better than the REIT’s prior midpoint and 125 bps better than beginning-of-year guidance, according to CFO Ben Fraker. The company was also “the only S&P 500 multifamily REIT to experience sequential improvement for both new lease rates and blended lease rates each quarter this year, and we were the only one with second- to third-quarter acceleration,” according to Jessett. Camden saw positive signs into Q4, though high-concession markets weighed on results. The REIT finalized its massive California sale and multiple acquisitions, though the interest rate environment forced it to cancel other deals. Rent trends Like many companies in supply heavy markets, Camden saw new leases remain in negative territory in Q3, falling to -2% YOY, according to its Q3 earnings release. In Q2, Camden’s new lease rate came in 130 bps lower at -3.3%. In Q3, renewals rose 3.6% YOY, giving the REIT a blended rate of 1%. In Q2, renewals increased 2.8% YOY and blends were -0.2%. “While renewal growth was in line with our expectations, new lease and blended lease growth were at the low end of our anticipated ranges, likely driven by the persistent concessions that remain in many of our core markets and sub-markets,” Camden Chief Operating Officer Laurie Baker said on the Q3 call. Camden sent out renewal offers to residents with December and January expirations at an average increase of 4.5%, according to Baker. That isn’t the only positive indicator. “We have seen signed new leases improve pretty dramatically in October as compared to September, and when we look at our October numbers and we compare them to October of last year, we're seeing really significant improvement,” Jessett said. Southeast Florida, at 1.6% YOY revenue growth; Atlanta, at 1.5%; Dallas, at 0.8%; and Houston, at 0.6%, were the top markets for Camden in Q3, according to a company Securities & Exchange Commission filing. Concessions have played a role in their performance, according to Baker. “We're seeing the strongest markets in Atlanta, Southeast Florida, Dallas and Houston,” Baker said. “And so, where those lower concessions are, we're obviously getting a little more pricing power, and we're having the ability to improve our occupancy.” On the other end of the spectrum were Denver, with a 5% YOY revenue decline; Nashville at -3.1%; Tampa, Florida, at -1.3%; and Orlando, Florida, at -0.7%, according to the SEC filing. “We still are continuing to see Denver and Nashville as those that have concessions that have been persistent,” Baker said. Buying and selling In July, Camden closed its sale of 11 properties with 3,620 apartment homes to a BlackRock-managed vehicle for $1.6 billion, recognizing a gain of $1 billion. The REIT used approximately $0.9 billion to retire balances outstanding under its unsecured revolving credit facility and commercial paper program, according to the Q3 earnings release. The REIT used $125 million to fund its August property and land acquisitions; $50 million to repurchase shares in August and early September; and $495 million toward the redemption of $500 million of senior notes due in November and to pay down borrowings in its commercial paper program. It had $55 million remaining in cash investment accounts for general corporate purposes, Fraker said on the call. In Q3, the REIT acquired Camden Brandon, a 296-unit property in Tampa; Camden LoSo, a 343-unit property in Charlotte, North Carolina; and Camden Gulch, a 300-unit property in Nashville, Tennessee, for a combined $305.2 million, according to the release. Camden acquired a land parcel in Tampa for approximately $18.3 million and sold 2.6 acres of land in Los Angeles for approximately $10.7 million, according to the release. Camden canceled the purchase of two properties and one land parcel in Q3 after interest rates rose , according to Jessett. “We went back looking for price adjustments, and clearly the sellers were not quite willing to capitulate to what we were looking for,” Jessett said. The REIT has also decided not to move forward with Nashville and Denver development projects at this time. items.title: October 2026 Jobs Report: Employment growth tops market forecasts
items.description: October 2026 Jobs Report: Employment growth tops market forecasts Written by Kenny Lee on November 6, 2026 Key findings U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while gains in September and August were revised up by a combined 84,000. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1% from 4.2% as strong employment growth absorbed an increase in labor force participation. Wage growth continued to cool compared to recent years, with average hourly earnings rising 3.1% year over year. What happened: The nonfarm payroll employment rose 165,000 in October, topping financial market expectations. Combined with strong upward revisions to increases in September and August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics report this month indicates a meaningful improvement in job growth. The increases in employment were broad-based across key industries such as professional and business services (+70,000); healthcare and social assistance (+55,000); and transportation and warehousing (+25,000). Employment in temporary help services, a leading indicator for overall labor demand, soared to 18,600. The household survey also indicates a resilient labor market. The labor force participation rate increased to 61.9% from 61.8% as more workers rejoined the workforce. Combined with strong increases in employment, the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%. Why it matters for housing: Stable employment and wage growth give households the confidence to buy a home or sign a new lease, but the housing market is already feeling the chilling effects of the recent surge in mortgage rates. Zillow data points to a colder-than-usual fall market: our preliminary measure of existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year in October. Newly pending listings — a leading indicator of next month’s closed sales — fell 16.8% year over year, the biggest decrease since August 2023. With mortgage rates above 7%, affordability headwinds in the housing market may still feel insurmountable — even for those who have a job or recently found one. This is consistent with our expectation for a more substantial decline in existing home sales and slower growth in home value in Q4. While mortgage rates have been declining from their recent peak, it is difficult to know how far they will fall when forces pushing up Treasury yields, such as anxiety over government deficits and geopolitical impact on energy prices, remain at play. But when mortgage rates come down, eventually, buyers will be ready. The Bureau of Labor Statistics report today is consistent with a stable labor market in a growing economy. The resilient labor market will pave the way for a housing market thaw. The region reported a 6.9% vacancy rate in the third quarter of 2026, down 60 bps YOY. Demand strengthened across all three counties, with total YTD absorption reaching 7,916 units. A total of 5,849 units have been delivered across the region thus far in 2026, while the development pipeline continues to moderate. Effective rents ended the quarter at $2.56 psf, up 0.1% YOY, reflecting continued stability despite elevated supply levels in recent years. Economy: Job Count and Unemployment Both Rise The Seattle metro area added 14,600 jobs year-over-year (YOY), with the latest total figure at over 2.1 million. The unemployment rate, however, also rose, up 40 basis points (bps) YOY to 5.0%, above the U.S. rate of 4.2%. items.title: From chaos to close: Holly Mabery says agents need to quell confusion
items.description: From chaos to close For agents, brokers and team leaders feeling overwhelmed by it all, Mabery said it's first important to remember that they are not going through this alone and that other agents and brokers are asking themselves the same questions. From there, the key to navigating the chaos, according to Mabery is figuring out what the most important things are and making them relevant to the person sitting in front of them. “I can't teach advanced geometry to a six-year-old. But I can show them the difference between a square and a triangle,” Mabery, a HousingWire Woman of Influence , Insider and Vanguard award winner, said. “The more you and I make things relevant and connect the dots for people, it becomes easier. But also I find that in connecting the dots, that trust layer opens up and everybody exhales.” In markets and environments currently experienced by real estate professionals, Mabery said it is easy to allow the chaos to turn in confusion. “When we have confusion, then there is no action as we lose opportunities. The more people are confused, the more they are afraid to move. It is like being stuck in really deep, thick mud,” she said. Noise vs. action To prevent this from happening with their agents and clients, Mabery said brokers and agents need to recognize what has happened and explain it using no jargon terms and then translate it to their specific market or situation by employing a noise versus action filter. This will allow them to understand what a national headline means for them and what actions they may need to take as a result. Mabery used an example of the Federal Reserve ’s rate hike in September, noting that most people feel this is a buyer problem and would have a conversation with their buy-side clients about how this impacts them and how they may need to change their offer strategy. But, Mabery said in her view it is actually a seller problem. “This is a seller problem because now, when less buyers feel like they can take action, it falls to the seller to take action,” Mabery said. “What are you willing to do in this market to actually make a difference to get people into your home and writing an offer?” People empowerment business When you provide consumers or even agents with information like this, Mabery says it enables them to feel empowered and hopeful. “As you look at 2027, I’m not scared for 3.8 million transactions, I’m just hunting for my piece of it,” Mabery said. With agents and brokers seriously contending with the possibility of a sub-4 million home sales environment in 2027, Mabery said it is important that agents and brokers find news and data sources they can trust, that they get back in touch with past-clients in their CRM and that they work on their story-telling skills. For Mabery, keeping client-facing messages short, personal and story-driven will enable agents to better connect with consumers and build trust. “The relationships you and I have are making all the difference in the world,” Mabery said. “The more confidence you build the more you inspire people to take action. When people are confused they stop taking action and we don’t sell anything and that is what we saw in 2026.” Despite this, Mabery noted that people still move and buy homes due to life events, inviting real estate professionals into their inner circles during some of the most exciting and trying times, but in order to be invited into these moments agents need to build trust in advance. “Take away the chaos and talk about what is next,” she said. “I want you to calm the fears as we go forward. The more you share your knowledge, your value goes up. And if I don't take action, is anybody hurt? No. But if I do, I get to help them.” Related More: eXp Realty

items.title: Mortgage rates ease as buyers gain leverage with concessions, ARMs
items.description: Mortgage rates eased slightly this week but stayed above 7.3%, keeping affordability tight and forcing loan officers to lean on seller concessions and adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) to close deals. At HousingWire ’s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, 30-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 7.35%, down from 7.38% one week earlier. Rates for 30-year jumbo loans averaged 7.56%, a 6-basis-point decline, while 30-year Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans were up 6 bps to 7.22%. “Since early October, rates have improved about 100 basis points, which can equate to an eighth of a point to 0.375, so that’s helping affordability," said Shannon Hoff, a California-based mortgage broker at Hoff Home Loans . Inflation remains a key obstacle. Data released Tuesday showed the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% on a monthly basis in October, hotter than expected, keeping the door open for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its December meeting. “Because that’s creating uncertainty, I am seeing buyers are still extremely payment-sensitive,” Hoff said. “However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, people were having to pay $100,000 over for the listing price. If your payment is going to change $100 or $200 from where you want the rate to be, in the big picture, that's not so worrisome.” First American senior economist Sam Williamson said hotter inflation is likely to prolong the wait for real mortgage rate relief. “ Stronger job growth may give some households the income to move, but elevated borrowing costs raise the hurdle for everyone,” Williamson said in a statement. “Until mortgage rates ease, life moves will keep the housing market moving, while discretionary buyers wait on the sidelines.” In this context, Optimal Blue 's October 2026 Market Advantage mortgage data report showed that rate-lock volume fell 19% month over month and 38% year over year. But ARMs represented 17% of total lock volume, the highest share in the report going back to 2019. "ARM share reached another high, FHA gained share and first-time buyers took a larger share across the major agency programs," Brennan O'Connell , director of data solutions at Optimal Blue, said in a statement. "For lenders, that means the opportunity is increasingly in helping borrowers find the product and payment structure that works for their circumstances." Buyer's market? As fewer borrowers are able or willing to buy at today’s rates, inventory is starting to build in parts of the country. That's giving buyers more leverage, while pushing sellers and builders to participate more heavily in financing costs. That’s the opposite of a few years ago, when rock-bottom rates, intense competition and limited supply forced buyers to bid far above list price and waive contingencies. “I'm licensed in nine states, I get to see various markets, and a lot of them are leaning toward the buyer,” said Gay Veale , a 30-year U.S. Air Force veteran and owner of Guidon Mortgage Group . “Because of that, there’s often seller concessions involved, and I am seeing people use those seller concessions for as many different ways to do rate buydowns or get their mortgage to be cheaper in the beginning, at least, if possible.” Veale cited one deal in which a borrower received $58,000 in seller concessions — an unusually high figure — and locked a 6% rate. With a 3-2-1 temporary buydown, a permanent buydown and an adjustable-rate mortgage, the borrower’s effective initial rate fell to 2.75%. “Around 75% of my clients are getting seller concessions. They're not all that much, but at least $10,000 is an average for me,” Veale said. Needs-based buyers Veale said most buyers using ARMs today are opting for products that provide about five years of lower rates before they reset . That roughly matches borrower expectations that rates could ease somewhat over the medium term. She added that most of her current clients are “need-to-move” borrowers rather than investors , such as people relocating for a job, dealing with a death in the family, welcoming a new child or trying to get closer to relatives. Investment purchases are far less common than during the pandemic period, she said. Veale said her business volume this year looks very similar to last year, an outcome she called “very atypical of the market” and not something she expects to see again under normal conditions. In Northern California , Hoff said weaker demand is allowing some buyers to negotiate steep price cuts and substantial credits. She pointed to a client scheduled to sign on Wednesday for a new home after securing $50,000 off the purchase price and $10,000 in seller credits. That $60,000 swing would have been unattainable in a hotter market, she said. “That $60,000 is much more than paying a half of a point or a point higher in rate," she said. "Not only is it the uncertainty affecting the buyers, it's also affecting the sellers." Down payment dynamics have shifted as well. During the pandemic, borrowers using down payment assistance or putting 3% down struggled to compete with cash offers and large down payments. Today, Hoff said, these buyers are reappearing. She is seeing “more first-time homebuyers jump in the market with challenged credit, down payment assistance, outside-the-box loans, bank statements . My loans are definitely a lot more challenging now.” Related More: 30-Year Fixed Mortgage Adjustable-Rate Mortgage Mortgage Rates Center

items.title: Former Trump Admin Officials Raise $130M For Modular Data Center Startup
items.description: Just months after being founded by three former Trump administration officials, modular data center startup Mavria has already reached a billion-dollar valuation as investors bet on its solution for the industry's supply chain woes: factory-built data centers. Pixabay/The Digital Artist The Texas-based company intends to mass-produce 5-megawatt modular data center units that are built in factories and delivered by truck. Although the first units are still months away from production, Mavria has already raised $130M at a $1B valuation, The Wall Street Journal reported . Its investors include Paradigm, Liquid 2 and Critical Frontier, as well as public benefit corporation AMP. Mavria was founded this summer by Adam Blake, Nick Poradek and Seth Cohen, who met while working at the U.S. Department of Energy, where they focused on nuclear power. While at the department, the three say they identified a “strategic vulnerability” in the U.S.’s digital infrastructure build-out: strained supply chains, manufacturing capacity constraints and limited access to large blocks of power. Mavria’s business model is centered on the idea of addressing that problem through standardized, factory-built data centers. Its founders say this strategy can ease some of the physical supply chain bottlenecks that have contributed to data center construction continuing to trail significantly behind demand for these facilities. “Our power infrastructure, manufacturing capacity and supply chains are nowhere near ready to meet the demand from AI,” Blake told The Wall Street Journal. Mavria's modular product, which is branded as Terrain, consists of 5 MW units with power distribution, liquid cooling, control systems and server racks already integrated. The company describes Terrain as an effective plug-and-play data center system that can either be clustered with other modules to create a larger facility or be deployed individually to take advantage of locations where smaller pockets of grid capacity are available. The 35-employee startup is not yet producing units at scale. Its first units are being built at the company’s Houston factory, with plans to begin testing in 2027 before ramping up production later in the year. Mavria intends to pursue two business lines: selling the units directly and developing sites where Terrain systems could be deployed and operated. Beyond helping bypass supply chain constraints, its business model is appealing to investors because it can avoid the community opposition and political headwinds that are constraining large-scale data center development across the U.S. Paradigm Managing Director Alana Palmedo told The Wall Street Journal that while communities are pushing back against "mega projects," these modular units are less intrusive and can be deployed wherever small pockets of power are available. Mavria isn't the first firm to pursue modular solutions to the data center supply chain pinch. Modular, prefabricated components and off-site manufacturing have become essential strategies when building large-scale data centers, and an entire ecosystem of firms has emerged that manufacture shipping-container-sized, standalone data centers that can be deployed individually or grouped in larger installations. It’s a space that includes smaller edge specialists like Duos Edge AI and CenCore and major data center equipment manufacturers like Vertiv, Schneider Electric and Eaton Corp. items.description: Pexels/Lennard A pair of UK pension funds are in talks to buy a £340M UK build-to-rent portfolio from a joint venture between the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Greystar . Northern LGPS and Local Pensions Partnership Investments have teamed up for their second major rented residential acquisition, the Fizzy Living portfolio owned by the international JV, Green Street News reported . The portfolio comprises eight assets and 974 existing homes in and around London. It was one of the first BTR portfolios built in the UK. ADIA backed Thames Valley Housing in the creation of the portfolio, and Greystar bought out Thames Valley’s position in 2021. The pair appointed JLL to find a buyer earlier this year. At the end of last year, Northern and LPPI teamed up to take private PRS REIT , a single-family housing specialist, in a £1.1B deal. The company owns 5,478 homes, and the pair have created a housing investment platform called the UK Housing Partnership, run by Waypoint Asset Management, Green Street reported. When the Fizzy Living assets are added to that platform, Northern and LPPI will own 6,500 rental homes, making the partnership one of the biggest owners in the country, across two property types, urban BTR and single-family. Both investors are part of the tranche of newish pooled local government pension funds, which combined the assets and functions of myriad smaller local authority pension schemes. The aim is to mirror the sophistication and investment power of Canadian or Australian superannuation schemes. And these funds have been particularly interested in rented residential. Earlier this year, Border to Coast bought a £450M single-family-home portfolio from Blackstone ’s Leaf Living . items.title: West Palm Beach Commissioners OK Related Ross' Plans For Air Taxi Stop
items.description: Related Ross , led by billionaire developer and Miami Dolphins owner Stephen Ross , is one step closer to making flying taxis a reality in South Florida. Archer Aviation West Palm Beach commissioners unanimously approved amending the CityPlace development's rules to permit an electric air taxi landing pad — a vertistop — on top of Related Ross' Hibiscus parking garage during a city commission meeting on Monday afternoon . "This is the first step in the process and the vote reflects a shared commitment to forward looking infrastructure and innovative mobility technology," Related Ross Executive Vice President Jordan Rathlev said in a statement shared with Bisnow. "These types of initiatives are central to the infrastructure solutions that are critical to a growing region and provide additional options within the broader mobility network," he said. The approval comes after the Sunshine State was selected to be a part of the Federal Aviation Administration's new pilot program for electric vertical takeoff and landing vehicles, or eVTOLs, earlier this year and amid Ross' broader efforts to expand vertiports across his projects, stretching all the way to Boca Raton. Shutts & Bowen 's Roger Ramdeen represented Related Ross in the application and stated that the review of noise and flight plans would be conducted by the FAA. At that point, the West Palm Beach City Commission, made up of Mayor Keith James and commissioners Cathleen Ward, Christy Fox, Joseph Peduzzi, Stephen Sylvester and Shalonda Warren, would be able to review the plans again. "If we decide to move forward with the actual use of this, it will be because it comes back to us and we have determined that all of the things that we've heard make sense for our community, and we'll have further discussion at that point," Fox said at the meeting. While some residents at the meeting voiced their support, others donned light-blue shirts with "Save West Palm Beach" in capital letters. Those against the vertistop's approval voiced concerns over noise, flight paths and how eVTOLs interact with existing air vehicles and emergency procedures, and questioned why it needed to be downtown rather than at the airport. The vertistop, which landed recommended approval from the city's planning board in September, is planned for one of multiple locations Ross aims to incorporate into company projects and personal holdings after launching a partnership with San Jose-based Archer Aviation in December to build out infrastructure for its eVTOLs. Ross is planning additional locations at the Miami Dolphins' Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens and the Apogee Golf Club in Hobe Sound. Archer also tapped Dragon Global to develop a vertiport site at its planned Magic City Innovation District in Little Haiti. Rathlev said during a panel on eVTOLs at the Urban Land Institute 's fall meeting in October that operators are looking all over the state, including Boca Raton, a market Ross entered this year after purchasing the 1.7M SF Boca Raton Innovation Campus in September and a two-building office complex nearby in October . A Related Ross spokesperson said the company does not have current plans for Boca Raton. While the company is not looking to invest its own dollars in the infrastructure, Rathlev said onstage in Miami Beach that eVTOLs are an amenity that adds to the allure of West Palm Beach, which Ross has pledged $10B to build and invest in, including multiple office towers, condo and apartment buildings, and retail space. "This needs to be a business case that we can offer as something that adds value incrementally to our residents who are buying our condominiums or renting in our office buildings, or want to buy sponsorship dollars for the Dolphins," Rathlev said in October. A lot of the process in incorporating air taxis over the next 10 years is gaining approvals, educating municipalities on the technology and integrating it within mobility systems, Rathlev said. "At the end of the day, in our conversation with all the operators, this is going to be the Uber of the sky or the Lyft to the sky, and that's what we're excited about," he said. items.title: Power Scarcity Poses Problems For Charlotte Industrial Developers
items.description: Industrial developers in Charlotte are vying for power. Small-bay industrial projects and some build-to-suit sites in the region are competing for energy against data centers, large advanced manufacturers and other big power users, panelists said at Bisnow ’s Charlotte State of the Market event . But demand is surpassing availability. “There’s a lot of users that need smaller buildings that still have an amazing power demand,” Kirk Matthews, vice president for Frampton Construction, said at the event, held at The Westin Charlotte. “We’re seeing small product … 100K [SF], 150K [SF] that still need 10 megawatts, and they’re not data centers.” Unsplash/American Public Power Association Duke Energy , the primary power supplier in the Carolinas, predicted last year that through 2040, electricity demand across its two Carolina systems would rise 16% to nearly 60%, according to a report from the North Carolina Energy Policy Task Force. The increased demand stems from a surge in population growth in Charlotte, which added more than 20,000 people last year and is nearing 1 million residents. The region’s energy grid is aging but is taking on additional load growth as the data center boom continues, Axios reported . That demand could delay or cancel projects as regulators weigh how to balance energy needs, panelists said. “Our electrical grid is nowhere near what it needs to be,” Alan Lewis, managing partner at The Keith Corp., said at the Sept. 30 event. Unsplash/Winston Chen The rise in data center development across the U.S. is driving electricity demand, which is expected to more than double from 31 gigawatts in 2025 to 66 GW by 2027, according to Goldman Sachs Commodities Research. Access to power is becoming a key driver of where companies decide to build capital-intensive real estate projects in the U.S. Charlotte's industrial market faces other hurdles, including skyrocketing costs of materials like steel and concrete. But panelists cited power constraints as the most imminent problem. “It's everything,” Lewis said. “I mean, No. 1 on the list almost every single time is, ‘How much power do you have?’” Data Center Construction Is 'A Big Drain' Charlotte’s industrial market is experiencing strong leasing activity and stable rent growth, according to a CBRE report from the third quarter. The metro “remains attractive for industrial expansion,” with leasing activity at 3.2M SF, up 55.6% from the same period in 2025. Vacancy in the third quarter was 7.1%, down from 7.9% the previous year. But power availability is a primary challenge for the growing market. A single hyperscale data center facility can consume 20 MW to more than 100 MW of power, equal to powering 15,000 to 75,000 homes, according to IAEI Magazine . More than 100 data centers are operational across North Carolina, with around 40 of them in Charlotte, according to Data Center Map . Last month, Charlotte extended its 150-day moratorium on data center development by 11 months to give the city more time to develop policies and regulations around the digital infrastructure. Key concerns among data center opponents include power demands and rising utility costs. But data centers aren’t the only developments consuming energy from Charlotte’s grid. “The massive amount of data center construction, and all the reshoring and direct investment here in new industrial facilities, is a big drain,” Lewis said. He added that the mass conversion to electric vehicles in the area is putting even more “stress on the system.” At least one planned industrial project in the area was halted over electrical demands. In September, North Carolina regulators rejected Duke Energy’s proposal to build a $584M natural gas power plant near Hamlet that would generate about 255 MW by 2030, citing concerns over how residents would be protected from the project’s costs. “There are real challenges in accommodating the amount of demand for these larger, big investment-type projects that want to be in the Carolinas,” said Jordan Quinn, a partner at Trinity Capital Advisors who leads the firm’s industrial platform. Other industrial projects in the area are underway. Red Bull broke ground on a new $1.7B facility in Concord in September 2025, and Eli Lilly announced a $77M expansion to its manufacturing campus earlier this year. Allocating Megawatts Pexels/andres Nino Charlotte's skyline Charlotte’s small-bay development pipeline remains active, with approximately 1.5M SF expected to deliver this year and another 2.2M SF under construction, according to a Matthews report . These properties typically have an easier time securing power than larger sites due to their size limitations. But because of the increased energy demand, “the requirements for smaller manufacturers have just gotten more intense,” Lewis said. “Every park we have, every site we have, we try to get the best information we can on how much power we have available,” he said. When a developer plans to build out multiple buildings within an industrial park, it can be difficult to divide up megawatts. “You often find yourself saying, ‘Well, gosh, if I do this deal, I'm going to lose two-thirds of my power that I have for everything else,’” he said. Sometimes a site will end up requiring more power than developers initially predicted. In a 50K SF deal, a tenant may need 10K SF of office space for 50 people, Quinn said. Air-conditioning that space to bring those people in could require 10,000 amps of power. “It's just this incredible challenge as an owner of industrial real estate in the market to accommodate not only the tenants' needs but to get them in quickly, when [tenants] actually need the space,” Quinn said. “It's very, very, very tough.” Duke Energy executives are expecting a power surge next year, as 5.2 gigawatts for data centers will hit the grid beginning in the second half of 2027, according to The Charlotte Ledger . items.title: ARMs hit record 17% of locks: Pitch beyond the 30-year
items.description: ARMs hit record 17% of locks: Pitch beyond the 30-year By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published November 10, 2026, 1:57 p.m. EST | Updated November 10, 2026, 2:06 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: Homebuyers seeking immediate affordability relief who risk facing severe sticker shock. Expert Quote: "October's data show how much affordability is shaping the purchase market." — Brennan O'Connell, Director of Data Solutions, Optimal Blue Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. A growing share of borrowers flocked to adjustable-rate mortgages in October, providing clues about where business may lie as well as the impact that the current economic environment is having on consumer behavior. The share of adjustable-rate mortgage locks last month hit 17%, the highest since the data was first tracked in 2019, according to Optimal Blue's Market Advantage Report. The ARM portion of locks rose from 14% one month earlier. Processing Content The new high mark came at the same time total rate-lock volume tumbled 19% from September and 38% on a year-over-year basis, with numbers falling across all loan categories amid ongoing macroeconomic pressures . Purchase lock volume decreased to an 84% share, relative to total activity, with demand slipping 18% and 17% from the prior month and year. The downward pressure across loan types led Optimal Blue's market volume index to plummet to a reading of 77 compared to 94 in September. "October's data show how much affordability is shaping the purchase market," said Brennan O'Connell, director of data solutions at Optimal Blue, in a press release. In other data showing the momentum currently boosting ARMs, the Mortgage Bankers Association reported lenders expanded availability of such financing for borrowers, especially those with lower loan-to-value ratios compared with recent history. The offerings helped push MBA's Mortgage Credit Availability Index higher for the first time in three months. The trends suggest that opportunities in today's subdued housing market exist outside the standard fixed-rate loan as long as originators can work with borrowers to find solutions that fit individual needs. ARM originations have historically risen when fixed rates surge, providing buyers with affordability relief for at least the first few years of their mortgage. The loans come with an initial fixed interest rate lower than the 30-year average. "For lenders, that means the opportunity is increasingly in helping borrowers find the product and payment structure that works for their circumstances," O'Connell said. Supporting its findings, Optimal Blue pointed out Federal Housing Administration-backed loans also accounted for an expanding percentage of mortgage locks, and first-time homebuyers grew in the agency market. The FHA segment made up 20% of locks, while Department of Veterans Affairs-backed mortgages took an 11% share, both up from September. Meanwhile, conforming loans made up 46% of all October locks, while non-conforming transactions accounted for 22%, both declining from the prior month. First-time buyers nabbed 45% of conforming purchase locks, climbing from both the previous month and year. Non-qualified mortgages, which are also experiencing heightened demand this year, made up 12% of October loan production, edging down from September but up by 195 basis points over the past three months and 420 basis points year over year. Non-QM lock volume split in close-to-equivalent shares between debt service coverage ratio, bank-statement and expanded guideline programs. Mortgage lenders see expanded credit availability The MBA's credit index increased 0.4% between September and October to a reading of 107.5, in part due to elevated ARM interest, with higher marks indicative of a greater number of products. In September, the MCAI settled at a score of 107.1, with a benchmark of 100 representing credit availability in March 2012, following the Great Recession. Unlike Optimal Blue's findings, though, government-product availability flattened, while conventional offerings grew, MBA reported. The uptick in ARM loans with lower LTV ratios included cash-out refinancing products, according to the trade association. "This also boosted the jumbo index, which was up to its highest level in three months," said Joel Kan, MBA vice president and deputy chief economist. The conventional MCAI increased 0.6%, while the government index grew by just 0.1%. Subindices within the conventional component showed jumbo offerings up 0.8% month to month and conforming credit unchanged. Look out for ARM regret Although lenders will appreciate the activity boosting their bottom line, recent history suggests consumers may want to approach them with caution. Research conducted in 2024 found approximately 70% of ARM borrowers expressed regret about their choice , with some facing sticker shock when the initial fixed term ended. items.title: Banks top JD Power originator ranking as digital drives satisfaction
items.description: Banks top JD Power originator ranking as digital drives satisfaction By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 10, 2026, 10:34 a.m. EST | Updated November 10, 2026, 1:50 p.m. EST 5 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight : Uncover how traditional banks dominated JD Power's latest mortgage origination satisfaction rankings. What's at Stake: Nonbank lenders fighting to retain market share against banks with pre-existing customer relationships. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. For the second consecutive year, banks occupied the top slots on JD Power's Mortgage Origination Satisfaction Study, benefitting from the importance of digital experiences to borrowers. The results reinforce findings in the Mortgage Servicer Digital Experience study released in October , where banks had the higher scores than the nonbanks graded. Processing Content A big part of the findings then was the banks had the advantage because of multiple product relationships. This is the case in the originator survey as well, said Bruce Gehrke, senior director of wealth and lending intelligence at JD Power. Customers looking for the trust factor "Digital is such a big part of the experience now, but it's also relationship based," Gehrke said. This creates a trust component with the banks. "I open up a checking and savings account or other accounts with a financial institution," he continued. "It takes a certain level of trust to do that, and it's not as big of a jump then to go for a loan as it would be to a completely unknown lender." This comes out in the data JD Power has for younger borrowers. But across the board some respondents consider it riskier to go to someone new for a mortgage. Originators that scored best in this year's survey Chase was the top scorer this year, at 789; It is a gain of 18 points over last year's 771. It was the top scorer in the servicer satisfaction survey released in the summer. Bank of America remained No. 2, but its score fell to 788 from 792. The bank rounding out the three was PNC, at 785, a significant jump from 721 one year ago, when it was third from the bottom. Tied for fourth at 776 were nonbanks Movement Mortgage and Rocket. Movement's score was unchanged from last year, where it was the top scoring independent mortgage bankers. Rocket's score increased from 762 one year ago. Citi, the only originator with a score over 800 last year at 802, was at 766 this year. This year's Originator Satisfaction survey returned an industry average of 760, equal to last year's findings. JD Power found improvements in digital channels and the ratings for lender staff were offset by declines in the level of trust established and opinions on keeping borrowers informed during the origination process. What changed from the 2025 results "I expected it to fall back a little, given the extra challenges we've seen this year, just financially certainly in the housing industry, and after such a large gain last year, where the majority of almost every lender was up and some really significantly," Gehrke said. The survey noted some of the friction is coming out of the process. For example, documents are now being sent directly to the lender from the source, rather than having to be emailed or copied. The process improvement is likely a result of the lower volume, leaving lenders with more capacity to deal with such things. "Some of the satisfaction indexes that we see in this study are higher than any other financial study that we have out there right now," said Gehrke. "So of all things in this environment, the mortgage origination process is really delivering." Furthermore, the business remains highly competitive and "competition drives improvement," he said. Which areas still can improve Still, a few negatives abound in the data. In particular, Power found 58% of those taking this year's survey said they received a same-day response for their lender, down 4 percentage points from 2025. While still at a relatively healthy 88%, the share who said they had a main point of contact for their mortgage fell from 91%. A larger share of borrowers experienced a problem after their loan was approved or when they went to closing.But what might give banks an advantage over nonbanks is those who had other financial products with the lender they applied to are more likely to trust that entity. This was to the point where they considered them a trusted advisor. When it comes to a digital experience, two-thirds of Gen Y and Gen Z mortgage borrowers preferred self-service tools for getting a loan; but almost half of the cohort added they wished their representative had been more involved. Gehrke pointed to other studies which show Chime opening more new checking accounts than the traditional banks, showing younger generations aren't necessarily tied to a relationship with those institutions that older demographics are. Yet the results also show that while they want better digital interactions, they also are looking for someone to be available to guide them if needed. Power added these borrowers are also significantly more likely to shop around, to the point where they use artificial intelligence tools when researching mortgage providers. This raises the stakes for lenders to deliver on both expectations, it added. In the overall business environment, banks have multiple business streams and this diversification puts them in a better position. But at the same time, Gehrke said they are not as willing to commit to residential real estate finance as much as an independent mortgage banker where it is the company's primary or only business line. But, he reiterated, competition drives better experiences for everybody and the data shows it bumping down the negatives in the housing industry right now. items.description: Hot inflation report puts Fed on track for December rate hike By Kyle Campbell CloseText About Kyle twitter ByKyleCampbell Published November 10, 2026, 8:53 a.m. EST | Updated November 10, 2026, 9:38 a.m. EST 4 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh. Bloomberg News Key insight: The latest CPI inflation report, which showed inflation rising 0.4% in October, puts more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates. Recent comments suggest policymakers will be ready to hike. Expert quote: " I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take." — Fed Gov. Christopher Waller Inflation rose faster than expected last month as lower energy costs could not offset broader price increases, according to Tuesday's consumer price index report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, rising 0.4% on the month. Processing Content The October CPI reading exceeded the consensus market forecast which expected a monthly increase of 0.24%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not issue an October CPI report last year, so the agency did not publish an annualized rate of inflation for last month. The print is better than September, when prices rose 0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year, but hints at a troubling trend of accelerating inflation. Ahead of the report, Federal Open Market Committee members were already expressing increased concern about prices. Hours before the report was released, Fed Gov. Christopher Waller said his baseline expectation was that inflation would improve from September but the committee will still raise its benchmark interest rate a quarter percentage point next month. Even if inflation had come in below 0.3%, Waller said in a pre-written speech delivered in London, he would have backed a 25 basis point hike. With the October reading coming in above that level, he could support a bigger increase. "I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting," Waller said. "That's my plan if things proceed as I expect. But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings … then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take." Waller joined the majority of FOMC voters in supporting their move to keep interest rates unchanged during the committee's meeting last month. In his speech he said this was appropriate because the group had already clearly signaled its intent to raise rates repeatedly, enabling market participants to price such a change into their valuation models. Yet, while the committee bought itself some flexibility in September, Waller said it must follow through on this "sooner rather than later" or else risk losing the trust of financial markets. Meanwhile, the Fed's other top priority, maintaining maximum employment, has been firmly in hand. The U.S. economy added 165,000 last month and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. Waller is not the only Fed official who has called for tighter monetary policy. Two FOMC participants voted against last month's policy hold, Fed Gov. Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack, both of whom preferred a hike. Cook has yet to explain her rationale. Hammack, in a speech delivered in Zurich, Switzerland last week, noted that inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for nearly six years and has recently shown signs of broadening out beyond volatile food and energy prices. Because of this, she, too, anticipates monetary policy being tightened. "I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2% in a timely manner," Hammack said. "I prefer getting to that stance through more frequent smaller adjustments when possible, something which would be less disruptive to households, businesses, and financial markets."
